items.name: Legal Aid application
items.text: Disposable income must be below £2,657/month and disposable capital below £8,000 (thresholds vary by case type).
items.action: Describe £2,657 as a joint gross monthly income limit rather than disposable income, and cite a source for thresholds varying by case type or remove it.
items.reason: Applying £2,657 to disposable income would tell people with gross income above the limit that they qualify when they do not.

problems.claim: Disposable income must be below £2,657/month and disposable capital below £8,000 (thresholds vary by case type).
problems.note: The figures match, but the text describes £2,657 as joint gross income (before deductions), not disposable income, and says nothing about thresholds varying by case type.

items.name: Statutory Redundancy Pay
items.text: Must have been continuously employed for at least 2 years and been made compulsorily redundant.
items.action: Drop the compulsory redundancy requirement and add the lay-off and short-time working route.
items.reason: This is a strict eligibility test, so the agent could tell people who were laid off, put on short-time working or not compulsorily dismissed that they do not qualify when they may.

problems.claim: Must have been continuously employed for at least 2 years and been made compulsorily redundant.
problems.note: The 2 years' continuous service is supported, but the text does not require compulsory redundancy: people who are laid off or put on short-time working can also qualify.

items.name: Repay a benefit overpayment
items.text: Must have been notified by DWP of a benefit overpayment.
items.action: Remove notification as a requirement and add that people who think they are being overpaid should report it.
items.reason: People who think they're being overpaid but haven't had a letter could be told the service isn't for them, and fail to report it as they must.

problems.claim: Must have been notified by DWP of a benefit overpayment.
problems.note: The text says you'll get a letter, but it doesn't make being notified a requirement. It even tells you to report an overpayment yourself if you think you're being overpaid.

items.name: Personal Independence Payment (PIP)
items.text: Must be aged 16 to 64 (under State Pension age). Those over 65 who did not have PIP before should claim Attendance Allowance instead.
items.action: Use State Pension age as the limit, and state the exception as getting PIP or ADP in the last 12 months.
items.reason: People aged 65 but under State Pension age would be wrongly sent to Attendance Allowance, and people who had PIP long ago would be wrongly told they can claim.

problems.claim: Must be aged 16 to 64 (under State Pension age). Those over 65 who did not have PIP before should claim Attendance Allowance instead.
problems.note: The text gives State Pension age, not 64 or 65, and makes the exception people who got PIP or ADP in the last 12 months, not anyone who ever had PIP.

items.name: Carer's Assessment
items.text: Any adult (18+) who provides regular and substantial unpaid care for someone with a disability, health condition, or frailty.
items.action: Drop 'substantial' and match the page's wording: an adult over 18 who regularly cares for someone ill, older or disabled.
items.reason: The 'substantial' test is not on the page and may be out of date, so carers doing less intensive care could be wrongly told they don't qualify.

problems.claim: Any adult (18+) who provides regular and substantial unpaid care for someone with a disability, health condition, or frailty.
problems.note: The text supports being over 18 and caring regularly for someone who is ill, older or disabled, but it does not say the care must be 'substantial' or 'unpaid'.

items.name: Council Tax Disability Reduction
items.text: Property must have at least one of: a room mainly used by the disabled person (not a bedroom, bathroom or kitchen); an extra bathroom or kitchen for the disabled person; extra space inside for wheelchair use.
items.action: Remove the bedroom exclusion and cite a source for the 'mainly used' condition.
items.reason: Excluding bedrooms would wrongly tell many typical applicants they don't qualify, such as those with a downstairs bedroom set aside for the disabled person, because the rules exclude only bathrooms, kitchens and toilets from the 'other room' route.

problems.claim: Property must have at least one of: a room mainly used by the disabled person (not a bedroom, bathroom or kitchen); an extra bathroom or kitchen for the disabled person; extra space inside for wheelchair use.
problems.note: The text supports the extra bathroom or kitchen, an other room, and wheelchair space, but it does not say the room must be mainly used by the disabled person or that bedrooms are excluded.

items.name: Disabled Persons Railcard
items.text: Receiving PIP (any component or rate), DLA, Attendance Allowance; or having epilepsy, registered severe visual/hearing impairment, or severe mental or physical disability requiring a companion.
items.action: Remove the companion-disability category, limit DLA to the qualifying rates, and change hearing impairment to evidence of deafness or hearing aid use.
items.reason: People getting lower-rate DLA or with unlisted disabilities would be wrongly told they qualify, and deaf applicants would be asked for a registration they don't need.

problems.claim: Receiving PIP (any component or rate), DLA, Attendance Allowance; or having epilepsy, registered severe visual/hearing impairment, or severe mental or physical disability requiring a companion.
problems.note: PIP, Attendance Allowance, epilepsy and visual impairment are stated. DLA qualifies only at certain rates. Hearing impairment needs evidence of deafness or hearing aid use, not registration. No category for severe mental or physical disability requiring a companion exists.

items.name: Adult Disability Payment
items.text: Must have a long-term physical or mental health condition or disability that affects daily living or mobility for at least 13 weeks and is expected to last at least 9 more months.
items.action: Cite the official eligibility guidance for the 13-week and 9-month condition duration rules.
items.reason: The duration test is a core qualifying rule, so if it were wrong, people with recent or short-term conditions would be told wrongly whether they qualify.

problems.claim: Must have a long-term physical or mental health condition or disability that affects daily living or mobility for at least 13 weeks and is expected to last at least 9 more months.
problems.note: The text supports the condition affecting everyday life, but it does not mention the 13-week or 9-month periods.

items.name: Voluntary National Insurance contributions (Class 3)
items.text: Under State Pension age, or within the window where contributions still count.
items.action: Remove the under-State-Pension-age requirement and keep only the 6-year deadline window.
items.reason: Many people filling gaps are at or over State Pension age, and they would be wrongly told they cannot pay Class 3 contributions.

problems.claim: Under State Pension age, or within the window where contributions still count.
problems.note: The 6-year deadline window is stated, but the text does not require you to be under State Pension age: people over it can pay Class 3.

items.name: Funeral Support Payment
items.text: Must be responsible for arranging or paying for a funeral.
items.action: Cite the official eligibility page stating that the applicant must be responsible for the funeral costs.
items.reason: This is a core eligibility rule, so if it were misstated, people could be told wrongly whether they qualify.

problems.claim: Must be responsible for arranging or paying for a funeral.
problems.note: The worked examples pay the person responsible for the funeral, but the text never sets out responsibility for arranging or paying as an eligibility rule.

items.name: Council Tax single person discount
items.text: Now living alone as the only adult (18+) in the property, following bereavement or separation.
items.action: Remove 'following bereavement or separation' so the criterion is just being the only adult (18+) living in the property.
items.reason: As a qualifying criterion, this would lead the agent to wrongly tell many people who live alone (for example, those who always have) that they don't qualify.

problems.claim: Now living alone as the only adult (18+) in the property, following bereavement or separation.
problems.note: The text supports living on your own and says you usually pay Council Tax from age 18, but it never mentions bereavement or separation.

items.name: Care to Learn
items.text: Parent must be under 20 at the start of the academic year.
items.action: Change the criterion to 'Parent must be under 20 at the start of their course'.
items.reason: This is the rule that decides eligibility, so measuring age on the wrong date would give wrong yes-or-no answers to parents who turn 20 between the start of their course and a later academic year.

problems.claim: Parent must be under 20 at the start of the academic year.
problems.note: The age limit of under 20 matches, but the source measures it at the start of the course, not the academic year.

items.name: Biometric Residence Permit
items.text: Granted a UK visa or leave to remain for more than 6 months.
items.action: Remove the 'more than 6 months' rule and state the 31 October 2024 cut-off, and say that BRPs have been replaced by eVisas.
items.reason: Anyone granted leave for more than 6 months would be wrongly told they qualify for a BRP, when BRPs have expired and been replaced by eVisas.

problems.claim: Granted a UK visa or leave to remain for more than 6 months.
problems.note: The text links holding a BRP to being granted permission to live or work in the UK, but it gives no 'more than 6 months' length and instead names a cut-off date of 31 October 2024.

items.name: Report an error with your eVisa
items.text: Has a UKVI account, including one the Home Office set up that you have never been able to sign in to.
items.action: Remove the general UKVI account requirement and keep only the case of an account set up by the Home Office that you have never signed in to.
items.reason: Making a UKVI account a condition for everyone could lead the agent to tell people without an account that they can't report wrong eVisa details, which the page does not say.

problems.claim: Has a UKVI account, including one the Home Office set up that you have never been able to sign in to.
problems.note: The text covers the case of an account the Home Office set up that you have never signed in to, but it never says a UKVI account is required for every case, such as reporting wrong eVisa details.

items.name: Register for Corporation Tax
items.text: All UK-registered limited companies, regardless of profitability or size.
items.action: Restrict the criterion to limited companies that are active and within the charge to Corporation Tax.
items.reason: Dormant or inactive companies would be wrongly told they must register.

problems.claim: All UK-registered limited companies, regardless of profitability or size.
problems.note: The text covers limited companies, but only those that are active and within the charge to Corporation Tax. It says nothing about profitability or size.

items.name: Register as sole trader
items.text: Has started to trade as a sole trader (self-employed), earning income from their own business.
items.action: Add the condition of earning more than £1,000 in a tax year and note that people can choose to register earlier.
items.reason: The criterion leaves out the actual trigger for registering, so the agent would wrongly tell low earners that they must register.

problems.claim: Has started to trade as a sole trader (self-employed), earning income from their own business.
problems.note: The text links registering to trading as a self-employed sole trader, but the stated trigger is earning more than £1,000 in a tax year, which the criterion leaves out, and the text also says you can choose to register earlier.

items.name: VAT registration
items.text: Taxable turnover has exceeded or is expected to exceed £90,000 in a rolling 12-month period.
items.action: Change the expected-turnover test to exceeding £90,000 in the next 30 days alone, and keep the rolling 12-month test for past turnover only.
items.reason: A business that only expects to pass £90,000 over the coming year would wrongly be told it must register now, and the correct 30-day trigger is left out.

problems.claim: Taxable turnover has exceeded or is expected to exceed £90,000 in a rolling 12-month period.
problems.note: The £90,000 threshold over the last 12 months is stated, but the text puts the expected-turnover test on the next 30 days, not a rolling 12-month period as the criterion says.

items.name: New Style ESA
items.text: Must have paid sufficient Class 1 or Class 2 NI contributions in both of the last two complete tax years.
items.action: Change to 'enough NI contributions, usually in the last 2 to 3 years, and credits count' and remove the unsourced Class 1/Class 2 rule.
items.reason: People relying on NI credits, or whose contributions fall in different years, could be wrongly told they don't qualify.

problems.claim: Must have paid sufficient Class 1 or Class 2 NI contributions in both of the last two complete tax years.
problems.note: The text requires enough NI contributions 'usually in the last 2 to 3 years' and says credits count; it names no Class 1 or Class 2 contributions and no 'both of the last two complete tax years' rule.

items.name: Discretionary Assistance Fund (Wales)
items.text: EAP: extreme financial hardship or an unexpected crisis with no other money. IAP: must get Income Support, income-based JSA, income-related ESA, Pension Credit Guarantee Credit or Universal Credit, and be leaving an institution, avoiding going into one, setting up home after an unsettled way of life, moving because of relationship breakdown or domestic abuse, or caring for a released prisoner.
items.action: Cite the official DAF eligibility guidance for the IAP qualifying benefits and situations and for the 'no other money' condition.
items.reason: These conditions decide whether a person qualifies for the IAP, and if any benefit or situation is wrong, applicants would be told wrongly whether they qualify.

problems.claim: EAP: extreme financial hardship or an unexpected crisis with no other money. IAP: must get Income Support, income-based JSA, income-related ESA, Pension Credit Guarantee Credit or Universal Credit, and be leaving an institution, avoiding going into one, setting up home after an unsettled way of life, moving because of relationship breakdown or domestic abuse, or caring for a released prisoner.
problems.note: The EAP hardship condition is stated, but the source gives no IAP benefit requirements or qualifying situations, and does not mention having no other money.

items.name: Give notice of marriage
items.text: Both parties must be 18 or over (16-17 with parental consent in exceptional circumstances).
items.action: Remove the 16-17 parental consent exception.
items.reason: The minimum marriage age in England and Wales is 18 with no exceptions, so a 16 or 17 year old would wrongly be told they could qualify and might try to give notice.

problems.claim: Both parties must be 18 or over (16-17 with parental consent in exceptional circumstances).
problems.note: The text supports the rule of 18 or over, but says nothing about 16-17 year olds marrying with parental consent.

items.name: Apply for teacher training
items.text: Must have, or be working towards, a UK undergraduate degree (2:2 or above).
items.action: Replace with 'a degree or equivalent qualification' and drop the UK-only and 2:2 conditions unless an official source supports them.
items.reason: People with overseas degrees or degrees below a 2:2 would be told wrongly that they are not eligible, even though the pages accept a degree or an equivalent.

problems.claim: Must have, or be working towards, a UK undergraduate degree (2:2 or above).
problems.note: The text asks for a degree or an equivalent, but it does not say the degree must be from the UK, give a 2:2 minimum, or mention people still working towards a degree.

items.name: Immigration fee waiver
items.text: Must demonstrate that payment of the visa fee would leave you (or your family) destitute or at risk of destitution.
items.action: Reword to match the source: no money for housing or essential living costs, or very low income where paying would harm a child's wellbeing.
items.reason: Low-income parents who are not destitute could be told wrongly that they do not qualify, because the child wellbeing route is left out and the 'destitution' wording sets a higher bar than the source.

problems.claim: Must demonstrate that payment of the visa fee would leave you (or your family) destitute or at risk of destitution.
problems.note: The text describes not being able to afford the fee because you lack housing or essential living costs, which is close to destitution, but it never says 'destitute' or 'at risk of destitution', and it adds a separate route: very low income where paying would harm your child's wellbeing.

items.name: Immigration fee waiver
items.text: Must be applying for a qualifying leave to remain or citizenship application.
items.action: Remove citizenship applications and name only the qualifying permission-to-stay routes.
items.reason: Citizenship applicants would be told wrongly that their application qualifies for a waiver.

problems.claim: Must be applying for a qualifying leave to remain or citizenship application.
problems.note: The text supports applications for permission to stay (leave to remain) on certain routes, but it says nothing about citizenship applications.

items.name: Maternity Allowance
items.text: Payslips or accounts
items.action: Remove 'accounts' and state that original payslips are required.
items.reason: Self-employed people, a main group for this service, may think they must send, or can send, accounts instead of the original payslips the page requires.

problems.claim: Payslips or accounts are needed.
problems.note: Original payslips are required, but the page never mentions accounts.
problems.quote: You need to provide original payslips as proof of income.

items.name: Employment Tribunal claim
items.text: Out of time — more than 3 months since incident
items.action: Say the limit is usually 3 months, that it runs from the end of employment for unfair dismissal, and that the clock is paused during Acas early conciliation.
items.reason: Most claimants go through Acas, which pauses the clock, so a typical person could wrongly think they are out of time and not claim.

problems.claim: A claim is out of time if more than 3 months have passed since the incident.
problems.note: The text says 'usually', starts the clock at the end of employment for unfair dismissal, and pauses the time limit during Acas conciliation, none of which the field mentions.
problems.quote: You usually have to make a claim within 3 months of your employment ending or the problem happening.

items.name: Legal Aid application
items.text: Domestic abuse victim in family proceedings with supporting evidence
items.action: Add the condition that the victim cannot afford legal costs, and drop the limit to family proceedings.
items.reason: Domestic abuse victims would be told they qualify whatever their means. Victims in other kinds of cases would be wrongly left out.

problems.claim: Domestic abuse victim in family proceedings with supporting evidence
problems.note: The text covers victims with evidence who cannot afford legal costs, but it does not limit this to family proceedings and adds the affordability condition.
problems.quote: You might be able to get legal aid if you have evidence that you or your children have experienced domestic abuse and you cannot afford to pay legal costs.

items.name: Legal Aid application
items.text: CW2 means test form
items.action: Correct this to CW2 (IMM) for immigration exceptional case funding only, or cite the correct general means form.
items.reason: Most applicants would be told to provide an immigration form that does not apply to them, mislabelled as a general means test form.

problems.claim: CW2 means test form
problems.note: The text only names form CW2 (IMM), for immigration exceptional case funding cases, and does not call it a means test form.
problems.quote: Immigration cases that go to a court or tribunal Complete the ECF application form CIV ECF 1 and form CW2 (IMM) .

items.name: Notify DVLA of medical condition
items.text: Relevant medical reports or confirmation from GP
items.action: Replace with 'Your GP or consultant's name and address; DVLA may contact your doctor', and remove the requirement for medical reports.
items.reason: Most drivers would think they must get medical reports or GP confirmation before reporting, which they don't need, so they could delay reporting or waste time and money.

problems.claim: Relevant medical reports or confirmation from GP
problems.note: The text says you may need to give your GP or consultant's name and address, and that DVLA might contact your doctor, but it does not say you provide medical reports or GP confirmation when you first report.
problems.quote: If you report your condition to DVLA through the service, you might need to give your GP or consultant’s name and address.

items.name: Access to Work
items.text: Evidence of employment or job offer
items.action: Replace with workplace address and a workplace contact who can confirm employment, or a UTR if self-employed.
items.reason: Applicants would gather employment documents they don't need and might not have the workplace contact details or UTR that the application asks for.

problems.claim: Evidence of employment or job offer is needed.
problems.note: The source asks for a workplace address and a workplace contact who can confirm you work there (or a UTR if self-employed), not documents proving employment or a job offer.
problems.quote: details of a workplace contact who can confirm you work there, if you're employed (they will not be contacted without your permission)

items.name: Carer's Allowance
items.text: Person cared for receives enhanced rate PIP daily living and carer works fewer than 16 hours
items.action: Replace 'enhanced rate' with 'any rate' and replace the 16-hour work limit with the £204 a week earnings limit.
items.reason: Carers of people on the standard rate would be wrongly turned away, and carers would be judged on hours worked instead of earnings, so many would be told the wrong answer on eligibility.

problems.claim: You qualify if the person you care for gets the enhanced rate of the PIP daily living component and you work fewer than 16 hours.
problems.note: The text accepts the PIP daily living component at any rate, not only the enhanced rate, and sets an earnings limit of £204 a week rather than a limit of 16 working hours.
problems.quote: Personal Independence Payment - daily living component

items.name: Disability Living Allowance (Child)
items.text: Medical evidence of disability or condition
items.action: Remove the general medical evidence requirement and mention form SR1 only for the end-of-life route.
items.reason: Typical parents would be told they must get medical evidence that the pages do not require, which could delay or put off claims.

problems.claim: Medical evidence of the disability or condition is needed.
problems.note: The only medical evidence mentioned is form SR1, and only for the end-of-life route; the text names no medical evidence requirement for ordinary claims.
problems.quote: Ask a medical professional for form SR1.

items.name: Personal Independence Payment (PIP)
items.text: Medical evidence from GP or specialist
items.action: Reword to say doctor's information is optional, include it if you have it, and drop the mention of specialists.
items.reason: Claimants would think they must get GP or specialist evidence before claiming, which could delay or put off their claim.

problems.claim: Evidence includes medical evidence from a GP or specialist.
problems.note: The text says to include information from your doctor if you have it, but it is optional and specialists are not mentioned.
problems.quote: Include supporting documents if you have them - for example, prescription lists, care plans, or information from your doctor or others involved in your care.

items.name: Blue Badge
items.text: Application to local council
items.action: Replace it with applying online through the GOV.UK Blue Badge service, noting that the council makes the decision.
items.reason: People acting on this would try to apply directly to the council instead of through the GOV.UK service, so they would be sent the wrong way to apply.

problems.claim: You make an application to your local council.
problems.note: The council makes the decision, but the text describes applying online through the GOV.UK service rather than to the council directly.
problems.quote: How you pay depends on your local council. They’ll usually make a decision within 12 weeks.

items.name: Carer's Assessment
items.text: No formal documentation required — contact local authority adult social care to request
items.action: Remove the 'no formal documentation required' claim and list the information the page says you'll need.
items.reason: Carers told they need nothing would contact adult social care without the details the page says they'll need, which could slow or complicate their request.

problems.claim: No formal documentation is required; you contact local authority adult social care to request the assessment.
problems.note: The text supports contacting adult social services, but it lists information you'll need and never says that no documentation is required.
problems.quote: You'll need: your NHS number (if you have one) your GP's name, address and phone number

items.name: Disabled Facilities Grant
items.text: Occupational Therapist assessment
items.action: Remove the OT assessment from required evidence and say the council may arrange an assessment by an OT or trained assessor.
items.reason: A typical applicant could delay applying or pay for a private OT report they do not need to provide.

problems.claim: Occupational Therapist assessment
problems.note: An assessment may happen, but it could be by a trained assessor instead, and the text does not say it is required.
problems.quote: The council may send an occupational therapist or trained assessor to see you.

items.name: Notify OPG of death
items.text: Death certificate
items.action: Say a death certificate is needed only if the person died outside the UK.
items.reason: Most people reporting a death in the UK would be told to send a document the official pages only ask for when the death was abroad.

problems.claim: A death certificate is needed.
problems.note: The text asks for a death certificate only if the person died outside the UK, not in every case.
problems.quote: If the donor or attorney died outside of the United Kingdom, you must also send a copy of the death certificate.

items.name: SR1 form (Special Rules for terminal illness)
items.text: Terminal diagnosis with 12-month prognosis
items.action: Replace with 'progressive disease where the clinician would not be surprised if the patient lived less than 12 months', and say no specific prognosis is needed.
items.reason: Patients without a formal 12-month prognosis could wrongly be told they do not qualify for Special Rules.

problems.claim: Terminal diagnosis with 12-month prognosis
problems.note: The test is a progressive disease where the clinician would not be surprised if the patient lived less than 12 months, and no specific prognosis is needed.
problems.quote: You do not need to give a specific prognosis.

items.name: Housing Benefit
items.text: Proof of rent (tenancy agreement)
items.action: Limit this to private landlord tenants and list a rent book or a letter from the landlord as alternatives.
items.reason: Council and housing association tenants would be asked for proof they don't need, and private tenants without a tenancy agreement wouldn't know other documents are accepted.

problems.claim: Proof of rent, such as a tenancy agreement, must be provided as evidence.
problems.note: The text only asks for this if you rent from a private landlord, and a rent book or a letter from your landlord can be used instead of a tenancy agreement; the claim leaves out that condition.
problems.quote: If you rent from a private landlord You’ll also need to provide one of the following: a tenancy agreement or rent book a letter from your landlord confirming your tenancy

items.name: Winter Fuel Payment
items.text: Born on or before 27 June 1960 and usually living in England, Wales or Northern Ireland (paid automatically with a listed benefit; otherwise you need to claim)
items.action: Say that people without a listed benefit only need to claim if they have not had the payment before or have deferred their State Pension since their last payment.
items.reason: Most pensioners without a listed benefit who were paid before will be paid automatically, but they would be told to make a claim they don't need.

problems.claim: Born on or before 27 June 1960 and usually living in England, Wales or Northern Ireland (paid automatically with a listed benefit; otherwise you need to claim)
problems.note: The birth date, residence and automatic payment with listed benefits are stated, but the text says people without a listed benefit need to claim only if they have not had the payment before or have deferred their State Pension since their last payment, not in every case.
problems.quote: You can get a Winter Fuel Payment if you were born on or before 27 June 1960 and usually live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland.

items.name: Warm Home Discount
items.text: Electricity account number
items.action: Limit the account number to people writing to the scheme after their supplier could not apply the discount.
items.reason: Listing it as required evidence means a typical person would be told to find an account number that the page doesn't ask for when applying or when the discount is automatic.

problems.claim: An electricity account number is needed as evidence.
problems.note: The page asks for the account number only when writing to the scheme because your supplier could not give you the discount; it does not ask for it when applying.
problems.quote: the name of your electricity supplier and your account number

items.name: Tell Us Once
items.text: Deceased's NI number and other details
items.action: Say the NI number is needed only for certain pension schemes and is otherwise optional.
items.reason: People would be told they must provide the deceased's NI number when it is usually optional, and those who can't find it may think they can't use the service.

problems.claim: You need the deceased's National Insurance number and other details.
problems.note: Other details of the person who died are required, but the NI number is only required for certain pension schemes and is optional otherwise.
problems.quote: You’ll also need their National Insurance number if they were getting money from or paying into any of the following pension schemes:

items.name: Obtain death certificates
items.text: Death registration reference number
items.action: Mark the GRO index reference number as optional and state the £3.50 extra search fee when it is not given.
items.reason: A typical applicant without the reference number would think they cannot apply, and would not be told they can still apply by paying £3.50 extra for each search.

problems.claim: A death registration reference number is needed as evidence.
problems.note: The text names a GRO index reference number, but it is optional: without it you pay £3.50 extra for each search.
problems.quote: If you do not have a GRO index reference number , you’ll have to pay £3.50 extra for each search.

items.name: Care to Learn
items.text: Parent aged 20 or over when academic year starts
items.action: Reword the exclusion to 'Parent aged 20 or over when their course starts'.
items.reason: This exclusion would wrongly rule out parents who turned 20 during their course, or whose course starts at a different time from the academic year, and stop them claiming childcare funding they are entitled to.

problems.claim: Parents aged 20 or over when the academic year starts are excluded.
problems.note: The source measures age at the start of the course, not the start of the academic year.
problems.quote: You must be aged under 20 at the start of your course.

items.name: National Insurance number
items.text: Biometric Residence Permit received and right to work confirmed
items.action: Make the right to work the only qualifier and note that BRP holders may already have a number.
items.reason: Tying qualification to a BRP could wrongly suggest that eVisa holders don't qualify, and could send BRP holders who already have a number to apply again.

problems.claim: Biometric Residence Permit received and right to work confirmed.
problems.note: The right to work is a stated condition, but the text never makes having a BRP a requirement; it only says BRP holders may already have a number.
problems.quote: If you have a BRP or eVisa, you might have a National Insurance number already.

items.name: Apply for a Gender Recognition Certificate
items.text: Medical reports from two registered medical practitioners
items.action: Change it to two reports from UK-registered doctors, or one doctor and one clinical psychologist.
items.reason: Applicants who already have a clinical psychologist's report could be told to get a second doctor's report they don't need, and nobody is told the practitioners must be registered in the UK.

problems.claim: Medical reports from two registered medical practitioners
problems.note: The source also allows one of the two reports to come from a clinical psychologist, so it does not require two medical practitioners, and the practitioners must be registered in the UK.
problems.quote: You need 2 reports written by either: 2 different medical doctors registered in the UK a medical doctor and a clinical psychologist, both registered in the UK

items.name: British citizenship (naturalisation)
items.text: Life in the UK test certificate
items.action: Replace 'test certificate' with the Life in the UK test unique reference number from the pass letter, and cite the official page that says this.
items.reason: Most applicants would look for a certificate they were never given (the test now gives a pass letter with a reference number), so they may be delayed or give the wrong evidence.

problems.claim: A Life in the UK test certificate is needed as evidence.

problems.note: PIP is not mentioned.

problems.claim: NHS prescriptions are free if you receive DLA.
problems.note: DLA is not mentioned.

problems.claim: NHS prescriptions are free if you receive ESA.
problems.note: ESA is not mentioned.

problems.claim: NHS prescriptions are free if you are on Universal Credit and have certain health conditions.
problems.note: Universal Credit is not mentioned.

problems.claim: NHS prescriptions are free if you are diagnosed with a qualifying medical condition.
problems.note: The eligibility check asks about health conditions, but the text never says a qualifying medical condition makes prescriptions free.
problems.quote: This service will ask about your age, where you live and any health conditions you have.

problems.claim: Qualifying conditions include diabetes, epilepsy and thyroid conditions.
problems.note: No specific conditions are named.

items.name: Carer's leave (employer)
items.text: Up to 5 days of unpaid leave per year from day 1 of employment to provide or arrange care for a dependant with a long-term care need. A statutory right since April 2024. Can be taken as individual days or half days.
items.action: Restate the entitlement as one working week every 12 months based on usual working pattern, and cite the April 2024 start date.
items.reason: The agent uses this to tell people their entitlement, so anyone who does not work a 5-day week would get the wrong amount of leave.

problems.claim: Up to 5 days of unpaid leave per year.
problems.note: The text gives one working week every 12 months, which depends on usual working pattern, not a fixed 5 days.
problems.quote: Employees can take up to one week of leave every 12 months. A ‘week’ means the length of time they usually work over 7 days.

problems.claim: It has been a statutory right since April 2024.
problems.note: The text gives no date the right started.

items.name: Disabled Persons Railcard
items.text: 1/3 off most rail fares for the holder and a companion. Qualifying conditions include receiving PIP, DLA, Attendance Allowance, being registered blind/partially sighted, or having epilepsy or severe mental or physical disability. Costs £20 for 1 year or £54 for 3 years.
items.action: Remove the 'severe mental or physical disability' category and list only the qualifying conditions the source gives.
items.reason: People with disabilities not on the list would be wrongly told they qualify.

problems.claim: Having a severe mental or physical disability qualifies.
problems.note: The source has no general 'severe mental or physical disability' category.

items.name: Adult Disability Payment
items.text: Scotland's replacement for Personal Independence Payment (PIP). For adults aged 16+ (under State Pension age) with a long-term physical or mental health condition or disability. Same rates as PIP. Assessed on impact of condition, not the condition itself.
items.action: Cite the official page for the age limits (16 to State Pension age), noting the exception for existing claimants over State Pension age.
items.reason: The age band decides who can apply, so if it were wrong, people would be told wrongly whether they qualify.

problems.claim: It is Scotland's replacement for Personal Independence Payment (PIP).
problems.note: The text describes moving from PIP to Adult Disability Payment but does not call Adult Disability Payment PIP's replacement.
problems.quote: you’ve moved from Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) Personal Independence Payment (PIP) to Adult Disability Payment

problems.claim: It is for adults aged 16 or over who are under State Pension age.
problems.note: The text gives no age limits for Adult Disability Payment; the only '16 or over' is for the vehicle leasing scheme.

problems.claim: It is paid at the same rates as PIP.
problems.note: The text never compares the rates with PIP.

items.name: Inherited State Pension (Additional or extra)
items.text: A widow, widower or surviving civil partner may inherit some of their spouse's Additional State Pension or protected payment. The amount depends entirely on the spouse's NI record and any deferral period, so no standard rate applies.
items.action: Replace the 'depends entirely on NI record, no standard rate' claim with the stated proportions, such as half of a protected payment.
items.reason: Survivors would get a wrong picture of what they will receive, because the official text sets a fixed share (half for protected payments) that this field contradicts.

problems.claim: The amount depends entirely on the spouse's NI record and any deferral period.
problems.note: The text does not say the inherited amount depends entirely on the spouse's NI record and deferral; for protected payments it says half is inherited.

problems.claim: No standard rate applies.
problems.note: The text does not say whether a standard rate applies to the inherited amount.

items.name: Pension Tracing Service
items.text: Free service available to anyone who has lost track of a workplace or personal pension. The service traces pension schemes and provides contact details so you can find out if you have a pension pot.
items.action: Replace 'anyone' with the actual conditions: it covers your own pension, or someone else's with their permission, and you need an employer or provider name. Also say the service gives contact details only and does not confirm whether you have a pension.
items.reason: Most users are not told they need an employer or provider name, people tracing someone else's pension are not told they need permission, and users are led to expect the service will confirm whether they have a pension pot.

problems.claim: The service is free.
problems.note: The text does not say whether the service is free.

problems.claim: The service is available to anyone who has lost track of a workplace or personal pension.
problems.note: The text covers your own scheme, or someone else's if you have their permission, and you need an employer or provider name; it does not say anyone can use it.
problems.quote: You need the name of an employer or a pension provider to use this service.

problems.claim: The contact details let you find out if you have a pension pot.
problems.note: The contact details are for searching for a lost pension, but the text says the service itself will not tell you whether you have a pension; it never says the details will confirm a pot.
problems.quote: This service will not tell you whether you have a pension, or what its value is.

items.name: State Pension claim
items.text: Not paid automatically — must be claimed. Apply up to 4 months before reaching State Pension age (currently 66). Full new State Pension (£241.30 a week) requires 35 qualifying NI years.
items.action: Replace the fixed age of 66 with a pointer to the State Pension age checker, and limit the 35-year rule to records that started after April 2016.
items.reason: The summary is the main answer most people see, and it combines three problems: the claim window is shown as universal, the age of 66 is wrong for people born after April 1960, and 35 years doesn't guarantee the full £241.30 for contracted-out or pre-2016 records, so many claimants would get the wrong timing or amount.

problems.claim: You can apply up to 4 months before reaching State Pension age.
problems.note: The 4-month window is given only for the phone route, not as a general rule for applying.
problems.quote: If you'll reach State Pension age in the next 4 months, you can phone the Pension Service to claim.

problems.claim: State Pension age is currently 66.
problems.note: The text never gives a figure for State Pension age.

problems.claim: The full new State Pension requires 35 qualifying NI years.
problems.note: The text gives 35 years only for records that started after April 2016. People who were contracted out usually need more than 35.
problems.quote: If your National Insurance record started after April 2016 you will need 35 qualifying years to get the full rate of new State Pension.

items.name: Funeral Support Payment
items.text: Help with funeral costs in Scotland for people on qualifying benefits. Usually covers the burial, cremation or hydrolysis cost in Scotland, plus £1,327.75 towards other funeral costs such as the service or funeral car (£162.05 if the person had a funeral plan), and help with some travel, transport, document and medical costs. Includes funerals for babies and stillborn babies. Apply from the death until 6 months after the funeral.
items.action: Cite the official pages for the qualifying benefits rule and for the application window from the date of death to 6 months after the funeral.
items.reason: The benefits requirement decides who qualifies and the window decides when people can apply, so if either is wrong, typical applicants would be misled.

problems.claim: It is for people on qualifying benefits.
problems.note: The text mentions low income but never says you must be on qualifying benefits.
problems.quote: Funeral Support Payment – help towards the cost of a funeral if you're on low income and live in Scotland

problems.claim: You can apply from the death until 6 months after the funeral.
problems.note: The 6-month limit appears only for the baby case, and the text never says applications can start from the date of death.
problems.quote: You must claim within 6 months of date of the funeral.

items.name: Oil and LPG heating payment (Wales)
items.text: One-off £200 payment (launched 31 March 2026) for low-income households in Wales who use heating oil or LPG and are on the Council Tax Reduction Scheme. Local authorities contact eligible households and invite them to apply; claims close 30 September 2026, 6 months after launch. People in severe hardship who do not qualify can apply to the Discretionary Assistance Fund.
items.action: Cite an official source for the 31 March 2026 launch date and the 30 September 2026 closing date.
items.reason: The specific deadline is worked out from an assumed launch date, so if that date is wrong, eligible households could be given the wrong last day to claim.

problems.claim: The payment launched on 31 March 2026.
problems.note: Only the press release's publication date is given; the text does not explicitly give a launch date.
problems.quote: First published: 31 March 2026

problems.claim: Claims close on 30 September 2026.
problems.note: The text gives a 6-month window, not the specific date of 30 September 2026.
problems.quote: There are 6 months from the scheme's launch to claim.

items.name: Cancel driving licence
items.text: Must notify DVLA when a driving licence holder dies. Usually handled automatically by Tell Us Once after death registration. Send the licence to DVLA if available.
items.action: Replace 'usually handled automatically' with a statement that you must tell DVLA yourself, by using Tell Us Once where available or by writing to DVLA.
items.reason: A bereaved person told it happens automatically may never notify DVLA, so they would miss a step they must take.

problems.claim: This is usually handled automatically by Tell Us Once after the death is registered.
problems.note: The text says you can use Tell Us Once to notify DVLA if it is available in your area, but it never says this is 'usually' done or 'automatic': you have to use the service yourself or with the registrar.
problems.quote: You can use the Tell Us Once service to notify DVLA when someone dies if it’s available in your area.

items.name: Order a birth, death or marriage certificate
items.text: Anyone can order certified copies of civil registration certificates from GRO for events registered in England and Wales. Certificates cost £12.50 each (sent 4 days after applying with a GRO index reference, or 15 working days without one, plus £3.50 per search). Priority service £38.50. Can also be ordered from the local register office.
items.action: Cite the official GRO page that says anyone can order certificates for events registered in England and Wales.
items.reason: The claim that anyone can order is the eligibility rule itself, so if it were wrong the agent would tell every applicant the wrong thing about whether they can order.

problems.claim: Anyone can order certificates.
problems.note: The text never says who is allowed to order certificates.

items.name: Apply for probate
items.text: Grants legal authority to deal with the estate. Required by most banks, insurers and financial institutions for estates over £10,000. Usually granted within 12 weeks of applying. Costs £526 for estates over £5,000; no fee for estates of £5,000 or less. Extra copies cost £2 each.
items.action: Remove the £10,000 threshold and say that copies cost £2 only when ordered with the application and £16 each after that.
items.reason: People could wrongly decide they don't need probate and could be quoted the wrong price for copies ordered later.

problems.claim: Most banks, insurers and financial institutions require probate for estates over £10,000.
problems.note: No £10,000 threshold appears; the text says every organisation has its own rules.

problems.claim: Extra copies cost £2 each.
problems.note: The £2 price applies only when copies are ordered with the application; copies ordered later cost £16 each.
problems.quote: You can order extra copies of the probate document for £2 each when you submit your application.

items.name: Inheritance Tax return (IHT400)
items.text: Required if the estate's value exceeds the nil-rate band (£325,000, or up to £500,000 with the residence nil-rate band). Tax must be paid within 6 months of death — before probate is granted.
items.action: Tie the requirement to tax being due, not just value, set the deadline as the end of the sixth month after death to avoid interest, and say payment normally starts before probate.
items.reason: Executors could be told wrongly whether they must file, could get the payment deadline slightly wrong, and could think the full tax must be paid before probate.

problems.claim: The IHT400 is required if the estate's value exceeds the nil-rate band of £325,000.
problems.note: The text makes full details depend on tax being due, not only on the value going over £325,000; exemptions can mean no tax is due above the threshold.
problems.quote: If Inheritance Tax is due You can use the online checker tool to find out if there’s Inheritance Tax to pay. If there is, you’ll need to send full details of the estate

problems.claim: Tax must be paid within 6 months of death.
problems.note: The text says by the end of the sixth month after death, not within 6 months, and gives this deadline as the way to avoid interest rather than a flat requirement.
problems.quote: You must pay Inheritance Tax by the end of the sixth month after the person dies to avoid paying interest.

problems.claim: Tax must be paid before probate is granted.
problems.note: The text says you normally have to start paying before probate, not that the tax must be paid in full first.
problems.quote: You’ll normally have to start paying Inheritance Tax before probate is granted.

items.name: Statutory Parental Bereavement Pay & Leave
items.text: Employees are entitled to 2 weeks of paid parental bereavement leave following the death of a child under 18 or a stillbirth after 24 weeks. Must be taken within 56 weeks of the death. Paid at the statutory flat rate.
items.action: State the pay conditions (26 weeks' continuous employment and £129 average weekly earnings) and the rate of £194.32 or 90% of average weekly earnings, whichever is lower.
items.reason: Bereaved employees could be told wrongly that they will be paid, or given the wrong amount, because the text says all eligible employees get pay at a flat rate.

problems.claim: Employees are entitled to 2 weeks of paid parental bereavement leave following the death of a child under 18 or a stillbirth after 24 weeks.
problems.note: The text supports 2 weeks' leave for a child dying before 18 or a stillbirth after 24 weeks, but pay has extra conditions (26 weeks' continuous employment and average earnings of £129 a week), so not every eligible employee gets paid leave.
problems.quote: You can take 2 weeks’ leave from the first day of your employment for each child who has died or was stillborn if you’re eligible .

problems.claim: It is paid at the statutory flat rate.
problems.note: The text gives a rate of £194.32 a week or 90% of average weekly earnings, whichever is lower, so the pay is not always a flat rate.
problems.quote: You may be entitled to either £194.32 a week or 90% of your average weekly earnings (whichever is lower).

items.name: Care to Learn
items.text: Available to parents under 20 (at the start of the academic year) who are in publicly funded education (school or college) and are the primary carer of a child. Covers childcare and travel costs to childcare.
items.action: Change the age test to 'under 20 at the start of the course' instead of the start of the academic year.
items.reason: Parents who were under 20 when their course started but are 20 at the start of a later academic year, such as second-year students on a two-year course, would wrongly be told they don't qualify.

problems.claim: Available to parents under 20 at the start of the academic year.
problems.note: The source ties the age limit to the start of the course, not the start of the academic year.
problems.quote: you’re a parent under 20 at the start of your course

items.name: Apply for or renew a passport
items.text: Any British national is entitled to a UK passport. First-time applicants need a countersignatory. Renewals can be done entirely online.
items.action: Reword to say British nationality is required but some British nationals are not entitled, that only paper applications need a countersignatory (online applications need someone to confirm identity), and that renewers may have to send their old passport or other documents.
items.reason: A typical person renewing online would be told the whole process is online and might not send their old passport or documents they are asked for, which could delay or stall the application. First-time applicants would also be told the wrong confirmation step for their route.

problems.claim: Any British national is entitled to a UK passport.
problems.note: The text makes British nationality a condition of eligibility, but it never says every British national is entitled, and it mentions people who are 'not entitled to a passport'.
problems.quote: Your child must have British nationality to be eligible for a British passport.

problems.claim: First-time applicants need a countersignatory.
problems.note: A countersignatory is only required for paper applications; online first-time applicants need someone to confirm their identity online, who does not sign a photo.
problems.quote: someone who can confirm your identity (a ‘countersignatory’)

problems.claim: Renewals can be done entirely online.
problems.note: The text says you can renew and pay online, but it does not say the whole process happens online, and applicants may be told to send supporting documents.
problems.quote: Use this service to apply for, renew, replace or update your passport and pay for it online.

items.name: Visa / leave to enter
items.text: Non-UK and non-Irish nationals wishing to enter the UK must apply for the appropriate visa. Type depends on purpose: work, study, family reunion, etc. Must usually be obtained before travel.
items.action: Change the wording to say non-British, non-Irish nationals must check whether they need a visa or an ETA, not that they must apply for a visa.
items.reason: Many typical travellers, such as visa-free nationals on short visits, would be told to apply for a visa they don't need and might not learn they need an ETA.

problems.claim: Nationals who are neither British nor Irish and want to enter the UK must apply for the appropriate visa.
problems.note: The page only tells non-British, non-Irish nationals to check whether they need a visa or ETA. It does not say they must apply for a visa.
problems.quote: Check if you need a UK Visa, electronic travel authorisation (ETA) or get access to an eVisa to prove your immigration status if you’re not a British citizen or Irish national

problems.claim: A visa must usually be obtained before travel.
problems.note: The page says nothing about getting a visa before travelling.

items.name: Electoral roll update
items.text: Register to vote at your new address. Affects eligibility for jury duty and credit checks. Can update online in 5 minutes. Also de-register from old address.
items.action: Remove the instruction to de-register from the old address and the claim that registration affects jury eligibility.
items.reason: People who move would be told to take a de-registration step the pages don't require, and the jury claim wrongly links registration to jury eligibility.

problems.claim: Being on the register affects eligibility for jury duty and credit checks.
problems.note: The text says the full register is used for credit checks and for jury summoning in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, but it does not say registration affects whether you are eligible for jury duty.
problems.quote: checking applications for loans or credit jury summoning in England, Wales and Northern Ireland

problems.claim: You should also de-register from your old address.
problems.note: The text says nothing about de-registering from an old address; it only says you can sometimes register at 2 addresses.

items.name: Apply for a postal vote
items.text: Available to registered voters in the UK who want to vote by post. Must apply at least 11 working days before the election. Photo ID is no longer required for postal vote applications but a National Insurance number or signature is needed.
items.action: Say that applicants must give both their National Insurance number (or other ID documents) and a signature, remove the photo ID claim, and cite a source for the application deadline.
items.reason: Applicants told a signature can replace their National Insurance number may send an incomplete application and have it rejected, and the application deadline is not confirmed by the pages checked.

problems.claim: You must apply at least 11 working days before the election.
problems.note: The text gives an 11 working day deadline for stopping a postal vote, applying for a proxy vote and changing the address, but gives no deadline for applying for a postal vote.

problems.claim: Photo ID is no longer required for postal vote applications.
problems.note: The text does not say whether photo ID is or was needed for postal vote applications.

problems.claim: A National Insurance number or a signature is needed.
problems.note: The text asks for a National Insurance number or other identity documents, and a signature photo as well, so the signature is not an alternative to the National Insurance number as the claim suggests.
problems.quote: your National Insurance number or other identity documents, for example a passport

items.name: Apply for a proxy vote
items.text: Available to registered voters who cannot attend a polling station on election day (due to work, illness, being abroad, disability, etc.). The proxy must be a registered UK voter. Deadline is 6 working days before the election for standard proxy; emergency proxy available up to 5pm on polling day.
items.action: Cite the official source for the 5pm, 6-working-days-before deadline and the 5pm polling-day emergency proxy deadline.
items.reason: Applicants rely on these deadlines to decide when to apply, so if they're wrong people could miss their chance to vote.

problems.claim: Reasons include work, illness, being abroad, disability, etc.
problems.note: The text mentions living abroad, but not work, illness or disability as reasons.
problems.quote: If you want to vote by proxy and you live abroad, apply for a proxy vote as soon as possible.

problems.claim: The deadline for a standard proxy is 6 working days before the election.
problems.note: The text gives no 6-working-day deadline. The only deadlines it gives are 11 working days, for changes and for switching from a postal vote.

problems.claim: An emergency proxy is available up to 5pm on polling day.
problems.note: The text mentions an emergency proxy but gives no 5pm-on-polling-day deadline.
problems.quote: If you miss the deadline to apply for a proxy vote before an election, you may be able to apply for an emergency proxy vote .

items.name: Student Finance (tuition fee + maintenance loans)
items.text: UK students starting an undergraduate course at a UK university can apply for a Tuition Fee Loan (up to £9,790 a year in 2026 to 2027, paid directly to the university) and a Maintenance Loan (income-assessed, to cover living costs). Repayments begin after graduating and earning over the threshold (currently £25,000/year). Applications open the year before study.
items.action: Limit the summary to students whose home is in England who meet the 3-year residence rule, remove or correct the £25,000 threshold for the current system, and drop the unsourced opening date.
items.reason: Students from Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland would be wrongly told they qualify here, and typical borrowers could be given the wrong repayment threshold.

problems.claim: UK students starting an undergraduate course at a UK university can apply for a Tuition Fee Loan and a Maintenance Loan.
problems.note: The source adds conditions the claim leaves out: your home must be in England and you must meet a 3-year residence rule.
problems.quote: Both of the following must also apply: your home is in England you’ve been continuously living in the UK, Channel Islands or Isle of Man for 3 years before the first day of your first academic year

problems.claim: The repayment threshold is currently £25,000 a year.
problems.note: The £25,000 figure appears only on the linked page about the new system for courses starting on or after 1 January 2027; the main page gives no figure for the current system.
problems.quote: For courses starting from 1 January 2027, you’ll start repaying your loans when you earn over £25,000 a year.

problems.claim: Applications open the year before study.
problems.note: The source gives no opening date for applications for this service.

items.name: Waste carrier, broker or dealer registration
items.text: Mandatory for all waste carriers, brokers and dealers in England. Two tiers: lower-tier (own waste only, free) and upper-tier (commercial waste handling, £191 to register, £130 to renew every 3 years). Changes to business details must be notified within 28 days. Separate registration schemes apply in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
items.action: Correct the tier definitions (own construction or demolition waste needs upper tier) and state the exact fees of £191.02 and £130.25.
items.reason: A typical trader carrying their own construction or demolition waste would be told they qualify for the free lower tier and would register in the wrong tier, and the fees are rounded.

problems.claim: Lower tier is for your own waste only and is free.
problems.note: The text says registration for transporting your own waste is usually free, but it does not tie this to the lower tier.
problems.quote: Registration is usually free if you only transport waste you produce yourself.

problems.claim: Upper tier is for commercial waste handling.
problems.note: The text mentions upper tier but never defines it as commercial waste handling.
problems.quote: If you have an upper tier registration, you must renew your registration every 3 years.

problems.claim: Registering costs £191.
problems.note: The text gives £191.02, and it does not tie the fee to the upper tier; the field rounds the figure.
problems.quote: Otherwise, registration costs £191.02.

problems.claim: Upper-tier registration must be renewed every 3 years at a cost of £130.
problems.note: The 3-year renewal is stated, but the fee is £130.25, not £130.
problems.quote: If you have an upper tier registration, you must renew your registration every 3 years. It costs £130.25.

items.name: Appeal to Tax Tribunal
items.text: Available to anyone who has received a decision from HMRC (on income tax, VAT, PAYE, penalties, etc.) and disagrees with it. Must appeal within 30 days of the HMRC review conclusion. No filing fee for most tax appeals.
items.action: Cite an official source for the no-fee claim and say that only most HMRC decisions can be appealed, not all.
items.reason: The fee claim affects what every appellant thinks they must pay, and 'anyone who disagrees' could wrongly tell people with non-appealable decisions that they qualify.

problems.claim: Anyone who has received an HMRC decision (on income tax, VAT, PAYE, penalties, etc.) and disagrees with it can use the service.
problems.note: The text names these taxes and penalty appeals, but it says only 'most' or 'some' decisions can be appealed, not every decision.
problems.quote: You can appeal against most decisions about ‘direct tax’ and ‘indirect tax’.

problems.claim: There is no filing fee for most tax appeals.
problems.note: None of the sources mention fees for filing an appeal.

items.name: Register for Corporation Tax
items.text: All limited companies must register for Corporation Tax within 3 months of starting to trade, even if making a loss. Applies to any company registered at Companies House.
items.action: Limit the duty to companies that are active and within the charge to Corporation Tax, and count the deadline from the start of the accounting period.
items.reason: Many newly formed or dormant companies registered at Companies House would be wrongly told they must register, and the deadline anchor is wrong.

problems.claim: All limited companies must register for Corporation Tax within 3 months of starting to trade.
problems.note: The duty only covers companies that are active and within the charge to Corporation Tax, not all limited companies, and the 3 months run from the start of the accounting period, not from starting to trade.
problems.quote: You must tell HMRC within 3 months of starting your tax accounting period if your limited company is within the charge of Corporation Tax and is now active.

problems.claim: Companies must register even if they are making a loss.
problems.note: The text says nothing about registering when making a loss.

problems.claim: It applies to any company registered at Companies House.
problems.note: The text does not say registration applies to every company registered at Companies House. It only covers active companies within the charge to Corporation Tax.

items.name: Making Tax Digital enrolment
items.text: Mandatory for all VAT-registered businesses — must keep digital records and file VAT returns via MTD-compatible software. Income Tax MTD rolls out from April 2026 for self-employed/landlords with income over £50k.
items.action: Cite the MTD for Income Tax guidance for the April 2026 date and £50,000 qualifying-income threshold, and mention the VAT exemptions.
items.reason: This is the main eligibility statement, so an unsourced threshold that does not say it means qualifying self-employment and property income, plus 'all' with no exemptions, could lead people to decide wrongly whether they must comply.

problems.claim: MTD is mandatory for all VAT-registered businesses.
problems.note: The text supports MTD being mandatory, but it allows exemptions, so 'all' is not fully backed.
problems.quote: HMRC will sign up all new VAT registered businesses to Making Tax Digital for VAT automatically unless they are already exempt or have applied for exemption.

problems.claim: Income Tax MTD rolls out from April 2026.
problems.note: The text does not mention Income Tax MTD or April 2026.

problems.claim: Income Tax MTD applies to self-employed people and landlords with income over £50k.
problems.note: The text does not mention self-employed people, landlords or a £50k threshold.

items.name: Register as sole trader
items.text: Anyone starting to work for themselves as a sole trader must register with HMRC. Done via the Self Assessment registration process. Deadline is 5 October in the second tax year of trading.
items.action: Add the £1,000 trading income threshold and cite an official source for the 5 October deadline.
items.reason: People earning £1,000 or less in a tax year would be told they must register when they do not have to, and the deadline they are given has no source.

problems.claim: Anyone starting to work for themselves as a sole trader must register with HMRC.
problems.note: The text only requires registration if you earn more than £1,000 in a tax year, and the claim leaves that condition out.
problems.quote: You can start trading straight away without registering. However, you must register for Self Assessment as a sole trader if you earn more than £1,000 in a tax year

problems.claim: The deadline is 5 October in the second tax year of trading.
problems.note: The text gives no registration deadline. It only says the tax year runs from 6 April to 5 April.

items.name: Road occupation licence (building work)
items.text: Required for any building work involving breaking or occupying a public road in England and Wales. Must contact the local authority directly — online applications are not accepted. Penalty for non-compliance: £10/day plus the council's remediation costs.
items.action: Remove the unsourced statement that online applications are not accepted and just say to contact the local council.
items.reason: Anyone who needs a licence could be told wrongly that they cannot apply online and be pushed away from the application route their council actually uses.

problems.claim: Online applications are not accepted.
problems.note: The text never says online applications are refused or unavailable.

items.name: Get a rod fishing licence
items.text: Required by law for anyone aged 13 or over fishing with a rod and line in rivers, streams, canals and some stillwaters in England and Wales. Fishing without a licence is a criminal offence. Junior licences (13 to 16) are free, and people aged 66 or over or disabled get a discounted 12-month licence.
items.action: Replace 'some stillwaters' with wording saying a licence is needed on all waters, private lakes included, and cite a source for the 'criminal offence' wording or change it to the £2,500 fine.
items.reason: Someone planning to fish a private lake or pond could be told they may not need a licence, then fish without one and risk a fine of up to £2,500.

problems.claim: The requirement applies to fishing in rivers, streams, canals and some stillwaters.
problems.note: The text says the licence is needed across England, Wales and the Border Esk, private lakes included, so it does not limit the rule to 'some' stillwaters.
problems.quote: This includes if you are fishing on private land, such as angling club waters or private fishing lakes.

problems.claim: Fishing without a licence is a criminal offence.
problems.note: The text mentions a fine of up to £2,500 but never calls fishing without a licence a criminal offence.
problems.quote: You can get a fine of up to £2,500 if you’re fishing in these areas and cannot show a valid rod fishing licence when asked.

items.name: Council Tax registration
items.text: Any adult who is the resident or owner of a domestic property is liable for Council Tax. Register at your new address and close the account at your old address. Various discounts and exemptions may apply.
items.action: Reword the liability sentence to match the official rules on who has to pay, and cite the moving guidance for the registration steps.
items.reason: Saying any adult resident or owner is liable is too simple (an owner who lives elsewhere usually pays only if nobody lives in the property), so people could be told wrongly that they must pay, and the steps for moving are unsourced.

problems.claim: Liability applies to the resident or owner of a domestic property.
problems.note: The text links the bill to adults living in a home and mentions paying on homes you own or rent, but it never says the resident or owner of a domestic property is the person liable.
problems.quote: A full Council Tax bill is based on at least 2 adults living in a home.

problems.claim: Register at your new address.
problems.note: The sources do not mention registering at a new address.

problems.claim: Close the account at your old address.
problems.note: The sources do not mention closing an account at an old address.

items.name: Local land charges search
items.text: Anyone can search for local land charges on a property in England. The search is typically done as part of property conveyancing. Searching is free; an official search certificate costs £15.
items.action: Say that the service covers England and Wales, that you must create an account first, and that not every area's data is on it yet (for those areas, search with the local council).
items.reason: Welsh users are wrongly told the service doesn't cover them, nobody is told they need an account, and people in areas whose data isn't on the service yet would be sent the wrong way to search.

problems.claim: Anyone can search for local land charges on a property.
problems.note: The text never says who can search, and it says you need to create an account first.

problems.claim: The search covers property in England.
problems.note: The service covers England and Wales, not only England as the claim implies, and not all data is on the service yet.
problems.quote: Use this service to check for local land charges in England and Wales.

problems.claim: The search is typically done as part of property conveyancing.
problems.note: The guide talks about buyers searching before they purchase and is aimed at conveyancers, but it never says the search is typically part of conveyancing.
problems.quote: if a purchaser makes an official or personal search before they purchase, they will generally be entitled to compensation

items.name: Sign your mortgage deed
items.text: Available to borrowers remortgaging or purchasing a property where the lender uses the Land Registry digital mortgage service. Requires a GOV.UK One Login account to verify identity before signing.
items.action: Limit eligibility to homeowners who are remortgaging, and remove the GOV.UK One Login requirement unless a source confirms it.
items.reason: People buying a property could be wrongly told they can sign digitally, and every user could be told to set up an account and identity check that the pages never mention.

problems.claim: It is available to borrowers buying a property.
problems.note: The text only mentions homeowners who are remortgaging and says nothing about purchases.

problems.claim: You need a GOV.UK One Login account to verify your identity before signing.
problems.note: The text names no account, sign-in or identity check.

items.name: Find an Energy Performance Certificate
items.text: EPCs are required by law when a property is sold or let. Buyers, tenants and homeowners can search the register for free. Landlords renting property in England and Wales must have an EPC rating of E or above.
items.action: Cite the private rented sector minimum energy efficiency standard guidance for the E rating and its exemptions, and cite the register page saying anyone can search it.
items.reason: Landlords in England and Wales use the E threshold to decide whether they can legally let a property, so an unsourced or wrong rating (or missing exemptions) could lead them to let unlawfully or make changes they don't need to.

problems.claim: Buyers, tenants and homeowners can search the register for free.
problems.note: The text says owners can check their own property and download the EPC for free, but it never says buyers or tenants can search the register.
problems.quote: Use the find an energy certificate service to check if your property has a valid EPC and download it for free.

problems.claim: Landlords renting property in England and Wales must have an EPC rating of E or above.
problems.note: The text mentions 'minimum energy performance requirements' for renting but never names a minimum rating of E.

items.name: New Style ESA
items.text: Contributory benefit for people whose health condition prevents or limits their ability to work. Requires NI contributions in the last two tax years and a fit note from a GP.
items.action: Change the contribution period to 'usually the last 2 to 3 years' and remove 'from a GP'.
items.reason: A typical claimant checking their NI record against the wrong years could decide wrongly whether they qualify.

problems.claim: It requires NI contributions in the last two tax years.
problems.note: The text says 'usually in the last 2 to 3 years', not strictly the last two tax years; it mentions the last 2 full tax years only when talking about reapplying.
problems.quote: paid enough National Insurance contributions, usually in the last 2 to 3 years

problems.claim: It requires a fit note from a GP.
problems.note: A fit note is needed only after more than 7 days off work, and the text does not say it must come from a GP.
problems.quote: a fit note (sometimes called a ‘sick note’ or a ‘statement of fitness for work’) if you’ve not been able to work for more than 7 days in a row

items.name: Prescription Prepayment Certificate (PPC)
items.text: Available to anyone in England who pays for NHS prescriptions and needs more than one item per month (3-month) or 12 or more items in 12 months (annual). Not available to those already exempt from prescription charges (e.g. UC claimants, over-60s).
items.action: Reword the item counts as break-even guides (4 or more items in 3 months, 12 or more in 12 months), not conditions for getting a PPC, and fix the UC exemption example.
items.reason: Anyone paying for prescriptions who needs fewer items than stated would wrongly be told they can't buy a PPC, and saying all UC claimants are exempt could wrongly put some people off buying one.

problems.claim: The PPC is available to anyone in England who pays for NHS prescriptions.
problems.note: The text states the England requirement but does not say it is open to anyone who pays for prescriptions.
problems.quote: You can only get a PPC if you live in England.

problems.claim: The 3-month PPC is for people who need more than one item per month.
problems.note: The text gives 4 or more items in 3 months as the point where a PPC may be cheaper, not as a condition for getting one, and it does not use a per-month figure.
problems.quote: if you’re going to buy 4 or more prescriptions in 3 months

problems.claim: The annual PPC is for people who need 12 or more items in 12 months.
problems.note: The text gives the figure of 12 or more in 12 months only as the point where a PPC may be cheaper, not as a condition for getting one.
problems.quote: or 12 or more prescriptions in 12 months, it may be cheaper to buy a PPC

problems.claim: The PPC is not available to people already exempt from prescription charges, such as Universal Credit claimants or people over 60.
problems.note: The text does not mention exemptions from prescription charges.

items.name: Best Start Foods
items.text: Paid every 4 weeks onto a prepaid card for buying healthy food: £22.40 during pregnancy, £44.80 for each child under 1, £22.40 for each child aged 1 to 3. For pregnant women and parents/carers of children under 3 in Scotland who receive a qualifying benefit. Some families with no access to public funds can also get it.
items.action: Cite the official 'Who should apply' page for the qualifying benefit requirement and its list of benefits.
items.reason: The qualifying-benefit condition decides whether a typical pregnant woman or parent qualifies, so if it is unsourced or wrong, people could be told wrongly that they qualify or don't.

problems.claim: You must receive a qualifying benefit to get it.
problems.note: The source text does not include a requirement to receive a qualifying benefit; the 'Who should apply' section is not in it.

items.name: Best Start Grant
items.text: Three one-off payments in Scotland for parents on qualifying benefits. Pregnancy and Baby Payment (£796.65 first child, £398.35 subsequent) from the end of the 24th week of pregnancy until the baby is 6 months old; Early Learning Payment (£331.95) between age 2 and 3½; School Age Payment (£331.95) in the year the child is first old enough to start school. Early Learning and School Age Payments are paid automatically to families getting Scottish Child Payment.
items.action: Cite a source for automatic payment to Scottish Child Payment families, and list the qualifying benefits.
