items.reason: Families would be told they need not apply for the Early Learning or School Age Payment, and the benefit requirement that decides eligibility is not stated, so if either is wrong people could miss payments or misjudge whether they qualify.

problems.claim: The payments are for parents on qualifying benefits.
problems.note: The text does not mention any qualifying benefits.

problems.claim: Early Learning and School Age Payments are paid automatically to families getting Scottish Child Payment.
problems.note: Neither the service page nor the linked Scottish Child Payment page says these payments are made automatically.

items.name: Scottish Child Payment
items.text: £28.20/week per child under 16 for the main person looking after the child in Scotland, if they or their partner get a qualifying benefit (Universal Credit, income-based JSA, Pension Credit, Income Support or income-related ESA). Child Benefit alone does not qualify.
items.action: Cite the official pages for the qualifying benefits list, the Scotland residency rule, the Child Benefit exclusion and how the carer is chosen.
items.reason: The list of benefits and the residency rule decide who qualifies, so any mistake would give parents the wrong answer on eligibility.

problems.claim: It goes to the main person looking after the child.
problems.note: The text says only one person can get it and that it is for children you look after, but it does not say the payment goes to the 'main' carer; instead it describes a separate process for deciding double claims.
problems.quote: Only one person can get Scottish Child Payment for a child.

problems.claim: The person must be in Scotland.
problems.note: The text does not state any requirement to live in Scotland for Scottish Child Payment.

problems.claim: The person or their partner must get a qualifying benefit: Universal Credit, income-based JSA, Pension Credit, Income Support or income-related ESA.
problems.note: The text does not list any qualifying benefits or name any of these benefits.

problems.claim: Getting Child Benefit alone does not qualify you.
problems.note: The text does not mention Child Benefit in relation to eligibility for Scottish Child Payment.

items.name: Discretionary Assistance Fund (Wales)
items.text: Emergency financial help in Wales. Two grants that do not need paying back: Emergency Assistance Payment for immediate crisis costs (food, gas, electricity, heating oil, emergency travel), and Individual Assistance Payment for furniture and white goods, applied for through an approved partner. Must be 16+ and live in Wales.
items.action: Say that heating oil claims under the EAP go through an approved partner, drop the claim that IAP is partner-only, and cite a source for the 16+ and Wales residency rules.
items.reason: Most IAP applicants would be told they can only apply through an approved partner, and heating oil applicants would not be told they need one, so both groups could be sent the wrong way to apply.

problems.claim: You apply for the Individual Assistance Payment through an approved partner.
problems.note: The source only says you must apply through an approved partner for heating oil (part of the EAP); it says nothing like this about the IAP.

problems.claim: You must be 16 or over.
problems.note: The source gives no age requirement.

problems.claim: You must live in Wales.
problems.note: The source does not state any residency requirement.

items.name: Marriage Allowance
items.text: Transfer up to £1,260 of unused Personal Allowance to your spouse/civil partner, saving up to £252/year in tax. Backdatable up to 4 years.
items.action: Replace 'up to 4 years' with the source's fixed backdating date of 6 April 2022.
items.reason: People claiming backdated tax years could be told they can claim for more years than allowed, which gives them the wrong refund amount.

problems.claim: A claim can be backdated up to 4 years.
problems.note: The source gives a fixed backdating date (6 April 2022), not a rolling limit of 4 years, so the '4 years' figure is not stated.
problems.quote: You can backdate your claim to 6 April 2022 (the 2022 to 2023 tax year) for any years you were eligible for Marriage Allowance.

items.name: SEND EHC plan assessment
items.text: An Education, Health and Care (EHC) plan for children and young people aged 0-25 with complex SEND needs that cannot be met through standard school support. Local Authority must complete the assessment within 20 weeks.
items.action: Say the council must decide within 16 weeks of the request whether to make a plan, and issue the final EHC plan within 20 weeks of the request.
items.reason: Families would get the wrong deadlines, expecting only the assessment to be done by 20 weeks, and could miss that the final plan is due by then and the decision by 16 weeks, which matters when they chase or challenge delays.

problems.claim: The local authority must complete the assessment within 20 weeks.
problems.note: The text's 20-week limit runs from the date the request is received and is for giving the final EHC plan, not for finishing the assessment, and the council only has to say within 16 weeks whether a plan will be made.
problems.quote: Your local authority has 20 weeks from the date they receive the request for the assessment to give you the final EHC plan.

items.name: Raise concerns about a school with Ofsted
items.text: Available to parents, staff, and members of the public with concerns about a school or further education provider in England. Ofsted will only consider concerns that reflect on the whole institution; individual pupil complaints must first be raised with the school directly.
items.action: State that complaints about individual pupils are outside the service, and remove the unsupported further education and England claims.
items.reason: A typical parent complaining about their own child would be told they can come to Ofsted once the school has dealt with it, when Ofsted will not consider individual complaints at all.

problems.claim: The service is available to parents, staff and members of the public.
problems.note: The text does not say who can use the service.

problems.claim: It covers concerns about a school or further education provider in England.
problems.note: State schools are covered, but the text does not mention further education providers or England.
problems.quote: Use this service to complain to Ofsted about a state school, including academies and free schools.

problems.claim: Complaints about individual pupils must first be raised with the school directly.
problems.note: The text requires everyone to complain to the school first, but it says complaints about individuals are outside the service altogether. It does not say they can come to Ofsted once the school has dealt with them.
problems.quote: your complaint is about things that affect the whole school, not individuals

items.name: Make a SORN
items.text: A free SORN must be made when a registered keeper stops taxing a vehicle and keeps it off public roads. The vehicle cannot be driven or parked on a public road — doing so can lead to prosecution and a fine of up to £2,500, and the vehicle may be clamped or impounded. SORN remains in place until the vehicle is taxed again.
items.action: Add the exception for driving to or from a pre-booked MOT or test, list sale, export and scrapping as ways a SORN ends, and cite sources for 'free' and for clamping or impounding.
items.reason: Keepers who need an MOT before taxing again would be told they cannot drive the vehicle at all, which is wrong about what they are allowed to do.

problems.claim: A SORN is free.
problems.note: None of the sources says whether making a SORN costs anything.

problems.claim: A SORNed vehicle cannot be driven or parked on a public road.
problems.note: The text allows driving to or from a pre-booked MOT or test, so an absolute ban on driving is not what it says.
problems.quote: You can only drive a vehicle with a SORN on a public road to go to or from a pre-booked MOT or other testing appointment.

problems.claim: The vehicle may be clamped or impounded.
problems.note: None of the sources mentions clamping or impounding.

problems.claim: The SORN stays in place until the vehicle is taxed again.
problems.note: The text also lists selling, permanently exporting or scrapping the vehicle as ways a SORN ends.
problems.quote: Your SORN is automatically cancelled when you tax your vehicle again or if you sell, permanently export or scrap your vehicle .

items.name: Criminal Injuries Compensation
items.text: Available to victims of violent crime in Great Britain who suffered a physical or psychological injury. Must claim within 2 years of the incident (exceptions for child abuse and some other circumstances). A tariff-based scheme from £1,000 to £500,000.
items.action: Correct the range to say injury payments are £1,000 to £250,000 and the maximum total award is £500,000.
items.reason: Claimants would be given the wrong tariff range and could expect an injury payment up to twice the real £250,000 limit.

problems.claim: Payments range from £1,000 to £500,000.
problems.note: The injury payment range is £1,000 to £250,000, and £500,000 is the maximum total award, which includes other payments such as loss of earnings, so the range in the claim mixes the two figures.
problems.quote: The maximum total compensation award is £500,000.

items.name: Contracts Finder
items.text: Free to use for any business or organisation looking to supply goods or services to the public sector. Contracts above £12,000 (central government) or £25,000 (other public bodies) must be published here.
items.action: Cite an official source that says Contracts Finder is free and gives the publishing thresholds and duty, or remove those claims.
items.reason: Every supplier is told the service costs nothing and that contracts above set values must be published here, so if the cost or the thresholds are wrong they would get wrong information about fees and about which contracts to expect.

problems.claim: Contracts Finder is free to use.
problems.note: None of the text about Contracts Finder says whether it costs anything; the 'free' support in Source 2 is general business advice, not this service.

problems.claim: Central government contracts above £12,000 must be published on Contracts Finder.
problems.note: The £12,000 figure (including VAT) is in the text, but nothing says publishing these contracts is compulsory.
problems.quote: Contracts Finder lets you search for information about contracts worth over £12,000 (including VAT) with the government and its agencies.

problems.claim: Contracts above £25,000 from other public bodies must be published on Contracts Finder.
problems.note: The text never mentions a £25,000 threshold or a publishing duty for other public bodies.

items.name: Apply for teacher training
items.text: Open to graduates (or those in their final year) with a 2:2 degree or above who want to qualify as a teacher in England. Routes include PGCE, School Direct, Teach First and SCITT. Entry requirements vary by provider.
items.action: Remove the 2:2 minimum, add teacher degree apprenticeships as a no-degree route, and only name routes the pages list.
items.reason: Non-graduates who could take a teacher degree apprenticeship, and graduates below a 2:2, would be told wrongly that they do not qualify.

problems.claim: The service is open to graduates, or people in their final year of a degree.
problems.note: The text says postgraduate training needs a degree, but it never mentions final-year students, and it says teacher degree apprenticeships need no degree at all.
problems.quote: Primary and secondary postgraduate teacher training qualifications You need the following or equivalents: a degree

problems.claim: Applicants need a 2:2 degree or above.
problems.note: The text asks for 'a degree' but never gives a minimum degree class.

problems.claim: Routes include PGCE, School Direct, Teach First and SCITT.
problems.note: None of these routes is named. The only kinds of training mentioned are postgraduate training, teacher degree apprenticeships and further education training.

problems.claim: Entry requirements vary by provider.
problems.note: The text gives some examples of provider discretion (equivalence tests, provider preferences, A level grades set by the university), but it does not say in general that entry requirements vary by provider.
problems.quote: The training provider may ask you to take an equivalence test or show other evidence of your ability.

items.name: National Careers Service
items.text: Free for anyone in England aged 13 or over. Provides one-to-one careers advice (phone, webchat, online), a skills assessment tool, job profiles and a course finder.
items.action: Cite the official page stating the service is free for people in England aged 13 or over.
items.reason: The England-only rule and the 13-or-over age limit decide who qualifies, so if they were wrong, typical users would be told wrongly whether they can use the service.

problems.claim: The service is free.
problems.note: The text never mentions cost.

problems.claim: The service is available to anyone in England.
problems.note: The text does not mention England or say who can use the service.

problems.claim: The service is for people aged 13 or over.
problems.note: The text gives no age limit.

items.name: Emergency travel document
items.text: Available to British nationals outside the UK who have lost their passport, had it stolen, or whose passport has expired and they need to return to the UK.
items.action: Say the passport must have recently expired, add the need to travel urgently within 6 weeks, and drop the requirement that the journey be back to the UK.
items.reason: People whose passport expired long ago, or who do not need to travel urgently, could be told they qualify when they do not, and people travelling to another country could wrongly think they are excluded.

problems.claim: It applies where the passport has been lost, stolen or has expired.
problems.note: The text says the passport must have recently expired, a condition the claim leaves out.
problems.quote: your UK passport has been lost, stolen, damaged, is full, has recently expired

problems.claim: The applicant needs to return to the UK.
problems.note: The text says you need to travel urgently within 6 weeks but does not say the journey must be back to the UK.
problems.quote: you need to travel within 6 weeks

items.name: Immigration fee waiver
items.text: Available to people applying for leave to remain or British citizenship who cannot afford the application fee. Must demonstrate financial need. The fee waiver does not apply to all visa categories.
items.action: Remove British citizenship applications from the summary.
items.reason: Typical adults applying for citizenship would be told wrongly that they can qualify for a fee waiver, and they would apply for one.

problems.claim: The waiver is available to people applying for British citizenship.
problems.note: The text never mentions British citizenship applications.

items.name: Appeal a visa or immigration decision
items.text: Available to people who have received a Home Office refusal that carries an in-country right of appeal. Not all decisions carry appeal rights. Must appeal within 14 days if in the UK or 28 days if outside.
items.action: Remove 'in-country' so the right of appeal covers appeals made from outside the UK.
items.reason: People refused while outside the UK could be wrongly told they don't qualify because their right of appeal isn't 'in-country', even though the page describes appeals from abroad.

problems.claim: Available to people who have received a Home Office refusal that carries an in-country right of appeal.
problems.note: The text requires a legal right to appeal but never says 'in-country', and it also describes appeals made from outside the UK.
problems.quote: You can only appeal to the tribunal if you have the legal right to appeal - you’ll usually be told if you do in your decision letter.

items.name: Child performance licence
items.text: Required for children below school-leaving age participating in public performances, sporting events, or professional modelling in England, Scotland and Wales. The event organiser (not the parent) applies at least 21 days before the event.
items.action: Add the conditions (paying audience, licensed premises or paid child) and cite a source for the nations covered.
items.reason: Organisers of events that don't meet the conditions would wrongly be told to apply for a licence at least 21 days ahead.

problems.claim: A licence is required for children below school-leaving age taking part in public performances, sporting events or professional modelling.
problems.note: The text says 'may need' and attaches conditions (a paying audience or licensed premises, or where the child is paid), which the claim leaves out.
problems.quote: A child may need a licence if they’re under school leaving age and taking part in: films, plays, concerts or other public performances that the audience pays to see, or that take place on licensed premises any sporting events or modelling assignments where the child is paid

problems.claim: This applies in England, Scotland and Wales.
problems.note: The text only says the rules differ in Northern Ireland; it never names England, Scotland or Wales as where the licence applies.
problems.quote: The rules are different in Northern Ireland .

items.name: Public film or TV screening permissions
items.text: Any public screening of films or TV — whether ticketed or free — requires a copyright licence, a premises licence from the local council, and a TV licence if using TV-receiving equipment. Multiple licences are typically needed simultaneously. Personal streaming subscriptions do not usually permit public screening; a commercial or business subscription may already give permission. State school curriculum use is exempt.
items.action: Change it to say a premises licence may be needed and that you may need one or more permissions, not that several are typically needed.
items.reason: Typical organisers would be told every public screening needs a premises licence and several licences, which pushes them to get permissions they may not need.

problems.claim: A public screening requires a premises licence from the local council.
problems.note: The text says a premises licence 'may' be needed, not that it always is.
problems.quote: You may need a ‘premises licence’ from your local council.

problems.claim: Multiple licences are typically needed at the same time.
problems.note: The text says you may need one or more permissions, but does not say that several are typically needed.
problems.quote: You may need one or more of the following:

items.name: Street collection licence
items.text: Required for any charitable collection in a public street or place in England and Wales. Free to obtain. Greater London collections (outside City of London) go through the Metropolitan Police. Penalty: £200 fine for collecting without a licence.
items.action: Cite an official source for the licence being free, or remove the fee claim, and say a licence may be needed depending on the council.
items.reason: The field tells every applicant the licence is free, but the official pages say nothing about a fee. Anyone whose council charges would be given the wrong cost, and everyone is told a licence is always required.

problems.claim: A licence is required for any charitable collection in a public street or place in England and Wales.
problems.note: The text covers England and Wales and public areas, but says a licence might be needed depending on the council, not that it is always required.
problems.quote: you might need a street collection licence, depending on your local council

problems.claim: The licence is free to obtain.
problems.note: The text does not mention any fee or say the licence is free.

items.name: Legal Aid application
items.text: Means and merits tested. Available in domestic abuse cases. Applied via Legal Aid Agency.
items.action: Say a legal adviser applies for you, and remove the Legal Aid Agency as the place to apply.
items.reason: Anyone reading this would try to apply to the Legal Aid Agency directly instead of going through a legal adviser. The merits-test wording is probably accurate and can be cited.

problems.claim: Legal aid is merits tested.
problems.note: The text says the problem must be serious, but it never calls this a merits test and never mentions assessing the case's prospects.
problems.quote: You’ll usually need to show that: your case is eligible for legal aid the problem is serious you cannot pay for legal costs

problems.claim: You apply through the Legal Aid Agency.
problems.note: The text says a legal adviser applies for you; it only mentions the Legal Aid Agency deciding exceptional case funding applications, not as the place you apply.
problems.quote: A legal adviser will apply for legal aid for you. You cannot apply for legal aid on your own.

items.name: Free childcare — 15 hours (3 and 4-year-olds)
items.text: Every 3 and 4-year-old in England gets 570 free hours a year (usually 15 hours a week for 38 weeks), from the term after their 3rd birthday. No income test and no application: arrange it with the childcare provider.
items.action: Cite the official page that says the universal 15 hours needs no application and is arranged directly with the childcare provider.
items.reason: This tells every parent how to get the entitlement, so if it were wrong they would skip a required application and lose the hours. It matches official guidance, so it needs a source rather than a rewrite.

problems.claim: No application is needed; you arrange it with the childcare provider.
problems.note: The text points parents to the provider or council to find out more, but it never says that no application is needed or that the provider arranges it.
problems.quote: Contact your childcare provider or local council to find out more.

items.name: Obtain P45 from employer
items.text: Employer must provide on last day. Required for new job or benefit claim.
items.action: Remove the last-day deadline and say a new employer can use the starter checklist instead of a P45.
items.reason: People leaving a job could wrongly expect the P45 on their last day, or think they cannot start a new job or claim benefits without one, when the starter checklist can be used instead.

problems.claim: The employer must provide the P45 on the employee's last day.
problems.note: The text says the employer should give a P45 when you leave, but it does not say this must happen on the last day or that it is compulsory.
problems.quote: When you leave a job, your employer should give you a P45 form

problems.claim: A P45 is required for a new job or a benefit claim.
problems.note: The text says to give the P45 to a new employer or to Jobcentre Plus for taxable benefits, but it also offers the starter checklist instead of a P45, so it does not say the P45 is required.
problems.quote: When you start a new job, give your P45 to your new employer. They use it to work out how much tax you’ll pay. If you’re not working and are claiming taxable benefits , give your P45 to the Jobcentre Plus.

items.name: Repay a benefit overpayment
items.text: Manage or repay a DWP benefit overpayment through an online account, direct debit or phone.
items.action: Remove the claims that DWP overpayments can be repaid online or by Direct Debit unless a DWP source confirms them.
items.reason: People repaying a DWP overpayment could try an online account or Direct Debit route that the sources don't show exists, and so repay the wrong way.

problems.claim: You can manage or repay a DWP benefit overpayment through an online account.
problems.note: The text only says you can report a Universal Credit overpayment through your account. It never says you can repay or manage one online.

problems.claim: You can repay a DWP benefit overpayment by direct debit.
problems.note: Direct Debit only comes up on the linked HMRC pages for tax credits and Child Benefit, which are different services, so DWP overpayments aren't covered.

items.name: Blue Badge
items.text: Auto-qualify on Enhanced Rate PIP mobility. Apply via local council.
items.action: Say that applications are made online through the GOV.UK Blue Badge service, and state the automatic eligibility rule exactly from the eligibility page.
items.reason: Applicants would be sent to their council instead of the GOV.UK service, and 'Enhanced Rate PIP mobility' does not match the actual automatic-eligibility rule (PIP points in specific activities), so some would be wrongly told they qualify automatically.

problems.claim: You automatically qualify if you get the Enhanced Rate of PIP mobility.
problems.note: The text says nothing about who automatically qualifies or about PIP rates.

problems.claim: You apply through your local council.
problems.note: The text says the council handles payment and decides, but the application itself is made online through this GOV.UK service, not directly to the council.
problems.quote: How you pay depends on your local council. They’ll usually make a decision within 12 weeks.

items.name: Disabled Persons Railcard
items.text: One third off most rail fares. Various disability benefits qualify automatically.
items.action: Remove 'qualify automatically' and state that proof such as an award letter is required.
items.reason: Benefit claimants may think they need no evidence and apply without the award letter they must upload.

problems.claim: Various disability benefits qualify automatically.
problems.note: The text lists qualifying benefits but requires proof such as award letters, and never says they qualify automatically.
problems.quote: You may be eligible for a Disabled Persons Railcard if you get support for a disability or long-term medical condition.

items.name: Inherited State Pension (Additional or extra)
items.text: A widow, widower, or surviving civil partner may be able to inherit some or all of their spouse's Additional State Pension (old system) or a protected payment top-up under the new State Pension, depending on when they reached State Pension age.
items.action: Say only part of the Additional State Pension can be inherited, and tie eligibility to when the deceased partner reached State Pension age, when they died and when the marriage began.
items.reason: Survivors would be told the wrong basis for qualifying (their own State Pension age) and could expect to inherit all of the Additional State Pension when only part can be inherited.

problems.claim: A widow, widower or surviving civil partner may be able to inherit some or all of their spouse's Additional State Pension (old system).
problems.note: The text says only 'part' of the Additional State Pension can be inherited; 'part of or all' is used only for extra State Pension or a lump sum from deferral.
problems.quote: You might inherit part of your deceased partner’s Additional State Pension

problems.claim: What can be inherited depends on when they reached State Pension age.
problems.note: The text makes inheritance depend mainly on when the deceased partner reached State Pension age (and when they died and when the marriage began), not on when the survivor reached it; the survivor's State Pension age matters only for remarriage.
problems.quote: your partner reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016

items.name: Funeral Support Payment
items.text: Usually covers burial, cremation or hydrolysis costs in Scotland, plus £1,327.75 towards other funeral costs (£162.05 if there was a funeral plan). Apply up to 6 months after the funeral.
items.action: Cite the official page that gives the general 6-month application deadline.
items.reason: Every applicant relies on this deadline, so if it is wrong, people could miss the real cut-off or be put off applying.

problems.claim: You can apply up to 6 months after the funeral.
problems.note: The 6-month limit is only given in the part about stillborn babies or babies who died shortly after birth, not as a general rule for every applicant.
problems.quote: You must claim within 6 months of date of the funeral.

items.name: Oil and LPG heating payment (Wales)
items.text: One-off £200 for households in Wales that heat with oil or LPG and get Council Tax Reduction. Councils contact eligible households; claims close 30 September 2026, 6 months after the scheme launched on 31 March 2026. Replaces the closed Winter Fuel Support Scheme.
items.action: Cite an official page that states the 30 September 2026 closing date and 31 March 2026 launch, and remove the unsourced Winter Fuel Support Scheme replacement claim.
items.reason: Applicants rely on the exact closing date, so an unconfirmed deadline could make someone miss the window; the replacement claim is only background.

problems.claim: Claims close on 30 September 2026.
problems.note: The text gives a 6-month window from launch but never names 30 September 2026 as the closing date.
problems.quote: There are 6 months from the scheme's launch to claim.

problems.claim: The scheme launched on 31 March 2026.
problems.note: The press release is dated 31 March 2026, but the text does not explicitly say the scheme launched on that date.
problems.quote: First published: 31 March 2026

problems.claim: It replaces the closed Winter Fuel Support Scheme.
problems.note: The text never mentions a Winter Fuel Support Scheme or says this payment replaces anything.

items.name: Apply for probate
items.text: Required if estate exceeds £10k with most financial institutions. £526 fee if the estate is over £5,000. Usually granted within 12 weeks.
items.action: Remove the £10,000 threshold and say each organisation sets its own rules.
items.reason: People with estates under £10,000 may be told they don't need probate when the bank or insurer holding the money still asks for it.

problems.claim: Probate is required by most financial institutions if the estate exceeds £10,000.
problems.note: The text gives no £10,000 threshold and says every organisation has its own rules.

items.name: Guardian's Allowance
items.text: £22.95/week per child, on top of Child Benefit, if raising a child whose parents have died (or one has died and the other cannot be found or is in prison or hospital). Backdatable 3 months.
items.action: Add the conditions that the surviving parent must be in prison for at least 2 years from the other parent's death, or detained in hospital by court order.
items.reason: Anyone whose surviving parent is on a short prison sentence or in hospital voluntarily would be wrongly told they qualify and might make a claim that gets refused.

problems.claim: You can get it if one parent has died and the other is in prison.
problems.note: The text requires the surviving parent to be in prison for at least 2 years from the other parent's death, and the claim leaves this out.
problems.quote: the surviving parent will be in prison for at least 2 years from the date of death of the other parent

problems.claim: You can get it if one parent has died and the other is in hospital.
problems.note: The text requires the hospital stay to be by court order, and the claim leaves this out.
problems.quote: the surviving parent is in a hospital by court order

items.name: Inheritance Tax return (IHT400)
items.text: If estate exceeds £325k threshold. Tax must be paid before probate is granted.
items.action: Say IHT400 is needed when tax is owed or full details are required, not just when the estate is over £325,000, and say payment normally has to start before probate rather than be made in full.
items.reason: Executors of estates over £325,000 left to a spouse could be told wrongly that they must file IHT400, and anyone who owes tax could think the full amount must be paid before probate.

problems.claim: The IHT400 is needed if the estate exceeds the £325k threshold.
problems.note: The text links IHT400 to Inheritance Tax being owed, not simply to an estate being over £325,000; estates above the threshold may owe nothing, for example when left to a spouse, and some estates must send full details even with no tax to pay.
problems.quote: If the estate owes Inheritance Tax, you must report its value within one year using form IHT400.

problems.claim: Tax must be paid before probate is granted.
problems.note: The text says you normally have to start paying before probate, not that the tax must be paid in full before probate is granted.
problems.quote: You’ll normally have to start paying Inheritance Tax before probate is granted.

items.name: Road occupation licence (building work)
items.text: Anyone digging up or placing materials, equipment or a skip on a public road in connection with building work must obtain a licence from the local council. Cannot be applied for online.
items.action: Remove the unsourced claim that the licence cannot be applied for online.
items.reason: Many councils take these applications online, so people applying could be sent away from their council's actual route and use a slower one instead.

problems.claim: Cannot be applied for online.
problems.note: The text only says to contact the council and never says whether online applications are possible.

items.name: DBS check
items.text: If working with children or vulnerable adults. Standard or enhanced check.
items.action: Reword to say anyone can get a basic check for any role, and that standard or enhanced checks are for specific roles such as work with children or in healthcare.
items.reason: Many people want a basic check for an ordinary job, and they could be told wrongly that they don't qualify because they don't work with children or vulnerable adults.

problems.claim: The check is for people working with children or vulnerable adults.
problems.note: The text gives children and healthcare as examples of roles that can get a more detailed check, but it also says any role can be checked, so the check is not limited to work with children or vulnerable adults.
problems.quote: For certain roles an employer can request a more detailed DBS check, for example if you'll be working with children or in healthcare.

items.name: Council Tax registration
items.text: Register at new address and close account at old. Various discounts may apply.
items.action: Cite the official page on telling your council when you move for the register-and-close-account steps.
items.reason: Anyone who is moving is told to do these two steps, so if the unsourced steps were wrong they would take the wrong action on their Council Tax account.

problems.claim: Register for Council Tax at your new address.
problems.note: None of the sources say anything about registering for Council Tax at a new address.

problems.claim: Close the Council Tax account at your old address.
problems.note: None of the sources mention closing an account at an old address.

items.name: Universal Credit
items.text: Main out-of-work or low-income benefit. Report change of circumstances within 1 month.
items.action: Remove the 1-month deadline and say to report changes straight away.
items.reason: Claimants may put off reporting a change for up to a month because of a deadline that doesn't exist, which can lead to overpayments they have to repay.

problems.claim: Changes of circumstances must be reported within 1 month.
problems.note: The text says to report changes but gives no 1-month time limit.
problems.quote: You should report a change of circumstances to get the correct payment.

items.name: Statutory Sick Pay (SSP)
items.text: Paid by the employer for up to 28 weeks: £123.25 a week or 80% of normal weekly earnings, whichever is lower. Paid for all full days off sick. There is no minimum earnings requirement.
items.action: Limit payment to full days off sick that the person would normally have worked, and cite a source for the claim that there is no minimum earnings requirement.
items.reason: Workers could expect SSP for days they would not normally work, such as weekends or non-working days, and so expect the wrong amount; the earnings claim decides who qualifies but has no source on this page.

problems.claim: SSP is paid for all full days off sick.
problems.note: The text limits this to full days off sick that you would normally have worked, and the claim leaves out that condition.
problems.quote: You’ll be paid SSP for all the full days you’re off sick that you normally would have worked.

problems.claim: There is no minimum earnings requirement.
problems.note: The text never says whether there is a minimum earnings requirement. It only says recent starters still qualify.

items.name: Scottish Child Payment
items.text: £28.20/week per eligible child under 16 for parents on qualifying benefits in Scotland, paid every 4 weeks.
items.action: Cite the official eligibility page for the qualifying-benefit and Scotland residency conditions.
items.reason: These two conditions decide whether anyone qualifies, so if they were wrong people would be told wrongly whether they can claim.

problems.claim: It is for parents on qualifying benefits in Scotland.
problems.note: The text never says you need a qualifying benefit or must live in Scotland to be eligible.

items.name: Renew driving licence
items.text: Renew a photocard driving licence when the photo expires (every 10 years) or after a name or address change. Separate from the mandatory age-70 medical renewal.
items.action: Remove address change as a reason to renew, and say that renewing after a name change is by post only.
items.reason: People who have only moved could be sent to the paid renewal service when they should use the separate change-of-address route. The 'medical' label for age-70 renewal is minor by comparison.

problems.claim: You renew the licence after a name or address change.
problems.note: The source covers renewing when your name has changed (by post only), but it never gives a name or address change as a reason to renew, and it doesn't mention address changes in the renewal context.
problems.quote: If your name or title has changed, you can only apply by post.

problems.claim: This is separate from the mandatory age-70 medical renewal.
problems.note: The source says age-70 renewal is a separate route and is required every 3 years, but it doesn't call it a medical renewal.
problems.quote: There’s a different way to: renew your licence if you’re 70 or over

items.name: Notify DVLA of vehicle sale
items.text: Sellers must notify DVLA the same day a vehicle is sold or transferred. Give the green new keeper slip from the V5C to the buyer. DVLA cancels the seller's tax and refunds any full months remaining. Buyer must tax the vehicle (or SORN it) before driving.
items.action: Remove the 'same day' deadline and say sellers must tell DVLA, without a specific time limit.
items.reason: Sellers are given a deadline the official pages don't set, so they get a wrong idea of what the law requires and when.

problems.claim: Sellers must notify DVLA the same day a vehicle is sold or transferred.
problems.note: The text says sellers must tell DVLA, but it gives no deadline and never says it must be the same day.
problems.quote: Tell DVLA when you no longer own a vehicle

items.name: Appeal a visa or immigration decision
items.text: Challenge a Home Office refusal of a visa, leave to remain or human rights application at the First-tier Tribunal (Immigration and Asylum Chamber).
items.action: Replace the general visa and leave to remain refusal wording with the specific appealable decisions the page lists.
items.reason: Most people with an ordinary visa or leave to remain refusal have no right of appeal, so they could be wrongly told they can appeal to the tribunal instead of asking for an administrative review or making a new application.

problems.claim: The decision challenged can be a refusal of a visa.
problems.note: Visa decisions come up in the page's heading, but the list of appealable decisions doesn't include a general visa refusal.
problems.quote: When and how to appeal against a visa, asylum or immigration decision

problems.claim: The decision challenged can be a refusal of leave to remain.
problems.note: The text only mentions refusal of leave for S2 healthcare visitors and refusal of status under the EU Settlement Scheme, not leave to remain refusals in general.
problems.quote: refuse or revoke your leave, or deport you if you’re an S2 healthcare visitor

items.name: Child performance licence
items.text: Children below school-leaving age taking part in public performances, sporting events or modelling require a licence from the local council. Applied for by the event organiser, not the parent.
items.action: Say a licence may be needed and add the conditions: a paying audience, licensed premises or the child being paid.
items.reason: Organisers and parents would be told every child performance, sporting event or modelling job needs a licence, when many unpaid or free events do not.

problems.claim: Children below school-leaving age taking part in public performances, sporting events or modelling require a licence from the local council.
problems.note: The text says a child 'may need' a licence and only under certain conditions (a paying audience or licensed premises, or where the child is paid), which the claim leaves out.
problems.quote: A child may need a licence if they’re under school leaving age and taking part in: films, plays, concerts or other public performances that the audience pays to see, or that take place on licensed premises any sporting events or modelling assignments where the child is paid

items.name: Public film or TV screening permissions
items.text: Showing films or TV in a public setting requires a copyright licence (e.g. from MPLC or Filmbank), a premises licence from the local council, and a TV licence if using TV-receiving equipment.
items.action: Say a premises licence 'may' be needed, and add that Northern Ireland may need a cinema licence instead.
items.reason: Many people screening films would think they always need a council premises licence and apply or pay for one they may not need, and people in Northern Ireland would not hear about the cinema licence.

problems.claim: Showing films or TV in a public setting requires a premises licence from the local council.
problems.note: The text says you 'may' need a premises licence, not that you always do, and says Northern Ireland may need a cinema licence instead.
problems.quote: You may need a ‘premises licence’ from your local council.

items.name: New Style Jobseeker's Allowance
items.text: Must have paid Class 1 NI contributions in both of the last two complete tax years before the year of claim.
items.action: Say Class 1 contributions for the last 2 tax years are usually needed, and that credits can count for one of those years.
items.reason: People with NI credits in one year, such as carers or people who were ill, could wrongly be told they don't qualify.

problems.claim: Must have paid Class 1 NI contributions in both of the last two complete tax years before the year of claim.
problems.note: The text says Class 1 contributions for the previous 2 tax years are usually needed, but it also says credits can count for one of those years, so it does not say you must have paid in both years.

items.name: Register the birth
items.text: Deadline is 42 days in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and 21 days in Scotland.
items.action: Cite the official Scottish source for the 21-day deadline.
items.reason: Parents in Scotland are the only group given an unsourced deadline, and a wrong deadline would affect when they register; the 42-day deadline for everyone else is supported.

problems.claim: Deadline is 42 days in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and 21 days in Scotland.
problems.note: The source supports the 42-day deadline but gives no 21-day deadline for Scotland.

items.name: Child Arrangements Order
items.text: Separated parents with children under 16 (or up to 18 if the order already exists).
items.action: Add that other relatives, such as grandparents, can apply, and cite or correct the age limits.
items.reason: Separated parents of younger children get the right answer, but grandparents and other relatives would wrongly be told they can't apply, and the unsourced age rule could mislead families with 16 to 17 year olds.

problems.claim: Separated parents with children under 16 (or up to 18 if the order already exists).
problems.note: The text says parents who separate can apply for a court order, but it gives no age limit for the child (neither under 16 nor up to 18 if an order already exists), and it also lets other relatives apply.

items.name: Divorce application (D8)
items.text: Must have been married or in a civil partnership for at least 1 year.
items.action: Change the criterion to say married for over a year, and cover civil partnerships under the separate process for ending a civil partnership.
items.reason: Married applicants get the right rule, but civil partners could be told they qualify for this divorce service when they must use a different route.

problems.claim: Must have been married or in a civil partnership for at least 1 year.
problems.note: The divorce page says you must have been married for over a year; the civil partnership condition comes from a linked page about a different service.

items.name: Employment Tribunal claim
items.text: Must have an employment dispute — unfair dismissal requires at least 2 years' service; discrimination claims have no service requirement.
items.action: Cite the official page stating that discrimination claims have no qualifying service period.
items.reason: The claim that discrimination needs no length of service is probably right but has no source, and it decides whether short-service workers think they can claim.

problems.claim: Must have an employment dispute — unfair dismissal requires at least 2 years' service; discrimination claims have no service requirement.
problems.note: The linked dismissal page gives the normal 2-year period for unfair dismissal, but the text never says discrimination claims have no service requirement.

items.name: Employment Tribunal claim
items.text: Must have an Acas EC certificate (early conciliation must be attempted first).
items.action: Say you must notify Acas and usually need a certificate, list the exceptions, and say that taking part in conciliation is optional.
items.reason: People who fall under an exception, or who don't want to conciliate, are told something they don't have to do, though most people still need to notify Acas and get a certificate.

problems.claim: Must have an Acas EC certificate (early conciliation must be attempted first).
problems.note: The text says a certificate is usually needed and lists exceptions; it also says you can choose not to take part in conciliation, so conciliation does not have to be attempted.

items.name: Cancel Marriage Allowance
items.text: Previously claimed Marriage Allowance and relationship has now ended (separated, divorced, or partner died).
items.action: Remove partner's death as a reason to cancel and cover bereavement as a separate case where the allowances change.
items.reason: Bereaved people would be wrongly told to cancel, when the page describes the allowances changing on death rather than asking for cancellation.

problems.claim: Previously claimed Marriage Allowance and relationship has now ended (separated, divorced, or partner died).
problems.note: Divorce, dissolution and legal separation are stated reasons to cancel, but a partner's death is not. The text treats death separately, describing how the allowances change rather than calling for cancellation.

items.name: Child Benefit transfer
items.text: Child has moved to live primarily with a different parent after separation.
items.action: Cite the rule that Child Benefit goes to the person the child lives with, and widen it beyond separated parents.
items.reason: Limiting this to a child moving between separated parents leaves out other carers, such as grandparents or relatives, who can also change who gets Child Benefit.

problems.claim: Child has moved to live primarily with a different parent after separation.
problems.note: The text links entitlement to living with the child, but it does not name a child moving to the other parent after separation as a condition for this service.

items.name: Child Benefit transfer
items.text: Parents have separated and current Child Benefit claimant is no longer the main carer.
items.action: Remove the condition that the current claimant must no longer be the main carer.
items.reason: Families where both people agree to switch the claimant, or where care is shared, would wrongly be told they can't change who gets Child Benefit.

problems.claim: Parents have separated and current Child Benefit claimant is no longer the main carer.
problems.note: The text covers families splitting up, but it never says the current claimant no longer being the main carer is a condition for changing who gets Child Benefit.

items.name: Shared Parental Leave & Pay
items.text: Mother must be eligible for SMP or Maternity Allowance for SPL to be available.
items.action: Reword the criterion so maternity leave entitlement also counts, and state the separate work and earnings test for the mother when the partner takes SPL.
items.reason: Some mothers are entitled to maternity leave but not SMP or Maternity Allowance, and some partners rely on the mother's work and earnings test. These families could wrongly be told SPL is not available.

problems.claim: Mother must be eligible for SMP or Maternity Allowance for SPL to be available.
problems.note: The text requires maternity leave and pay (or Maternity Allowance) to be cut short, but it never says the mother must be eligible for SMP or Maternity Allowance. Where the partner takes SPL, the mother's criteria are about work and earnings instead.

items.name: Statutory Paternity Pay
items.text: Continuously employed with the same employer for at least 26 weeks and earning at or above the Lower Earnings Limit.
items.action: State that the 26 weeks must be reached by the qualifying week, give the £129 average weekly earnings figure, and cite the page that links it to the Lower Earnings Limit.
items.reason: People who started their job recently may be wrongly told they qualify because the qualifying-week deadline is missing, and people may not know the actual earnings figure they need to meet.

problems.claim: Continuously employed with the same employer for at least 26 weeks and earning at or above the Lower Earnings Limit.
problems.note: The text supports the 26 weeks of continuous employment and gives the earnings test as an average of at least £129 a week, but it never mentions the 'Lower Earnings Limit' or links £129 to it, and the field leaves out that the 26 weeks must be reached by the qualifying week.

items.name: Income tax refund (P50)
items.text: Unemployed for 4 weeks or more, not claiming taxable state benefits, and not returning to work or starting a taxable pension in the same tax year — if you expect to start a new job within 4 weeks, your new employer will make any repayment through your salary instead.
items.action: Reword the pension condition to match the page's 'taxable income such as a works pension' wording, or cite a source for it.
items.reason: People who start a works or private pension in the same tax year could misjudge whether they can claim, because the page frames this as other taxable income rather than a named condition.

problems.claim: Unemployed for 4 weeks or more, not claiming taxable state benefits, and not returning to work or starting a taxable pension in the same tax year — if you expect to start a new job within 4 weeks, your new employer will make any repayment through your salary instead.
problems.note: The page says to check for taxable income, including a works pension, before the end of the tax year, but it does not name 'starting a taxable pension' as an eligibility condition.

items.name: Renew driving licence at 70
items.text: Must confirm at renewal that eyesight meets minimum standard and no medical condition prevents driving. DVLA may require medical evidence if a condition has been declared.
items.action: Cite the DVLA guidance saying applicants must declare eyesight and fitness to drive, and that DVLA may ask for medical evidence about declared conditions.
items.reason: Applicants with medical conditions need to know they must declare them and may be asked for evidence; this is probably accurate but is only partly sourced now.

problems.claim: Must confirm at renewal that eyesight meets minimum standard and no medical condition prevents driving. DVLA may require medical evidence if a condition has been declared.
problems.note: The text states the eyesight and fitness conditions and says DVLA may test your eyesight after a reported vision condition, but it does not say you must confirm these things, or that medical evidence may be required for any declared condition.

items.name: Attendance Allowance
items.text: Must have reached State Pension age (66 or over).
items.action: Cite the State Pension age guidance for 66 and note that the age is rising to 67.
items.reason: 66 is right today, but as State Pension age rises, some people who have turned 66 would wrongly be told they qualify.

problems.claim: Must have reached State Pension age (66 or over).
problems.note: The text requires State Pension age but never gives the age 66.

items.name: Disability Living Allowance (Child)
items.text: Must be in England, Wales or Northern Ireland (Scotland uses Child Disability Payment).
items.action: Say this service covers England and Wales, and send Northern Ireland families to the separate DLA for children in Northern Ireland application.
items.reason: Families in Northern Ireland would be sent the wrong way to apply, though families in England and Wales are not affected.

problems.claim: Must be in England, Wales or Northern Ireland (Scotland uses Child Disability Payment).
problems.note: England, Wales and the Scotland exclusion are stated, but Northern Ireland families are sent to a separate 'DLA for children in Northern Ireland' application rather than being covered by this service.

items.name: Mandatory Reconsideration
items.text: A DWP benefit decision has been received (e.g. UC, JSA, ESA, PIP award or change). Mandatory Reconsideration must happen before a tribunal appeal.
items.action: Add that some decisions can go straight to an appeal, and cite a source that names DWP.
items.reason: Anyone whose decision can go straight to an appeal would be told a reconsideration is required first.

problems.claim: A DWP benefit decision has been received (e.g. UC, JSA, ESA, PIP award or change). Mandatory Reconsideration must happen before a tribunal appeal.
problems.note: The text covers these benefits and says the notice comes before an appeal, but it never names DWP and it says some decisions can go straight to an appeal.

items.name: Personal Independence Payment (PIP)
items.text: Long-term physical or mental health condition or disability affecting daily living or mobility. Must have had difficulties for at least 3 months and expect them to continue for at least 9 months.
items.action: Cite the official source for the 3-month and 9-month periods, or reword to the 12-month expectation in the text.
items.reason: A wrong duration rule could make some people with recent or shorter-term conditions think they do or do not qualify.

problems.claim: Long-term physical or mental health condition or disability affecting daily living or mobility. Must have had difficulties for at least 3 months and expect them to continue for at least 9 months.
problems.note: The condition requirement is stated, but the text gives a single 12-month expectation and never mentions a 3-month qualifying period or a 9-month future period.

items.name: UC Carer element
items.text: Eligible for Carer's Allowance (caring 35+ hours/week for someone on qualifying disability benefit).
items.action: Remove the 'Eligible for Carer's Allowance' framing and keep the 35+ hours caring for someone on a listed benefit test.
items.reason: The bracketed test is correct, but the Carer's Allowance framing could lead the agent to apply Carer's Allowance conditions and wrongly exclude some carers.

problems.claim: Eligible for Carer's Allowance (caring 35+ hours/week for someone on qualifying disability benefit).
problems.note: The source supports caring 35+ hours a week for someone on a listed benefit, but does not frame this as Carer's Allowance eligibility.

items.name: Social Security & Child Support Tribunal
items.text: Mandatory Reconsideration must have been completed and the outcome confirmed in a Mandatory Reconsideration Notice from DWP.
items.action: Add the exception that some decision letters allow an appeal straight away without Mandatory Reconsideration.
items.reason: People whose decision letter lets them appeal directly would wrongly be told they don't qualify yet, although most people do need reconsideration first.

problems.claim: Mandatory Reconsideration must have been completed and the outcome confirmed in a Mandatory Reconsideration Notice from DWP.
problems.note: The linked page supports needing the notice, but the main page says some people can appeal straight away without reconsideration, and DWP is never named.

items.name: Carer's Credit
items.text: Not already receiving NI credits through Carer's Allowance, UC, or earnings above the Lower Earnings Limit.
items.action: Cite the official page confirming that Universal Credit claimants already get NI credits, or remove the Universal Credit reference.
items.reason: Carers on Universal Credit could be wrongly told they cannot get Carer's Credit, because the pages don't link Universal Credit credits to Carer's Credit eligibility.

problems.claim: Not already receiving NI credits through Carer's Allowance, UC, or earnings above the Lower Earnings Limit.
problems.note: The Carer's Credit page does not mention Universal Credit, and the linked Carer's Allowance page only says UC gives Class 3 credits, without linking that to Carer's Credit eligibility.

items.name: Disabled Facilities Grant
items.text: Property in England where the disabled person lives, whether owned, rented privately, or from a housing association.
items.action: Include Wales and Northern Ireland, and list owners, tenants and landlords where the disabled person intends to live.
items.reason: People in Wales or Northern Ireland would wrongly be told they don't qualify, and landlords are left out.

problems.claim: Property in England where the disabled person lives, whether owned, rented privately, or from a housing association.
problems.note: Owners, tenants and landlords can apply, and the disabled person must intend to live there. Housing associations are not mentioned, and the grant is not limited to England: Wales and Northern Ireland are also covered.

items.name: NHS Continuing Healthcare (CHC)
items.text: Primary health need assessed as complex, intense, or unpredictable — usually a progressive serious illness, terminal condition, or severe disability.
items.action: Cite the National Framework for the need characteristics and soften or source the 'usually progressive or terminal illness' examples.
items.reason: People with a primary health need that is not a progressive, terminal or severe-disability condition could wrongly think they are excluded and not ask for an assessment.

problems.claim: Primary health need assessed as complex, intense, or unpredictable — usually a progressive serious illness, terminal condition, or severe disability.
problems.note: The text requires a primary health need arising from disability, accident or illness, but it does not describe that need as complex, intense or unpredictable, and it does not mention progressive serious illness or terminal conditions.

items.name: Carer's leave (employer)
items.text: Must be an employee (not a worker or self-employed). Applies from the first day of employment.
items.action: Cite official carer's leave guidance that limits the right to employees, rather than relying on the parental leave page.
items.reason: Workers and self-employed people are told they do not qualify, based on a source for a different service, which affects whether they qualify.

problems.claim: Must be an employee (not a worker or self-employed). Applies from the first day of employment.
problems.note: The carer's leave page confirms employees qualify from day one but never says workers or self-employed people are excluded; that exclusion appears only on the linked parental leave page, which covers a different service.

items.name: Motability scheme
items.text: Receiving the Enhanced Rate of the Mobility Component of PIP (or equivalent: DLA highest rate mobility, AFIP or WPMS).
items.action: Cite the Motability eligibility page, change 'DLA highest rate' to 'higher rate', and add the Scottish Adult and Child Disability Payment equivalents.
items.reason: The list of allowances is probably correct, but calling it the 'highest' DLA rate is inaccurate and leaving out the Scottish benefits could lead the agent to wrongly turn away people in Scotland.

problems.claim: Receiving the Enhanced Rate of the Mobility Component of PIP (or equivalent: DLA highest rate mobility, AFIP or WPMS).
problems.note: The text mentions only a 'qualifying mobility allowance'. It does not name the PIP enhanced mobility rate, DLA higher rate mobility, AFIP or WPMS.

items.name: Carer Support Payment
items.text: Must live in Scotland.
items.action: Change to 'usually must live in Scotland' and add the EU/EEA and Armed Forces/Civil Service exceptions.
items.reason: Carers in the EU/EEA with a link to Scotland, or posted abroad in the Armed Forces or Civil Service, would wrongly be told they don't qualify.

problems.claim: Must live in Scotland.
problems.note: The text says carers usually need to live in Scotland, with exceptions for the EU/EEA area with a link to Scotland and for people posted abroad in the Armed Forces or Civil Service, so it is not an absolute rule.

items.name: Child Disability Payment
items.text: Child must have a physical or mental disability requiring substantially more care or supervision than a child of the same age, or have difficulty walking.
items.action: Cite the official test comparing the child with a child of the same age, or drop 'substantially' if no source supports it.
items.reason: The agent uses this criterion to decide eligibility, so an unsourced 'substantially more' threshold could lead it to wrongly turn away borderline applicants.

problems.claim: Child must have a physical or mental disability requiring substantially more care or supervision than a child of the same age, or have difficulty walking.
problems.note: The text states physical or mental disability with care, supervision or walking needs, but never compares these with a child of the same age or says 'substantially more'.

items.name: Notify OPG of death
items.text: A registered LPA exists and the donor has died.
items.action: Cite an official page saying the LPA must be registered, or drop the registration condition.
items.reason: People whose LPA was never registered could be told wrongly whether they need to contact OPG, though this is probably accurate.

problems.claim: A registered LPA exists and the donor has died.
problems.note: The donor's death is stated as the trigger, but the text does not say the LPA has to be registered for this to apply.

items.name: Notify OPG of death
items.text: Requires a registered LPA to be in place.
items.action: Cite an official page saying reporting a death applies only to registered LPAs.
items.reason: This rules out anyone whose LPA isn't registered on a condition the pages don't state, which matters to that smaller group.

problems.claim: Requires a registered LPA to be in place.
problems.note: The linked guide is about registered LPAs, but it never says reporting a death requires the LPA to be registered.

items.name: Pension Credit
items.text: Must have reached State Pension age (currently 66).
items.action: Cite the State Pension age guidance and note that the age is rising from 66 to 67.
items.reason: People born after April 1960 may be given the wrong qualifying age as State Pension age rises past 66.

problems.claim: Must have reached State Pension age (currently 66).
problems.note: The source says you must have reached State Pension age but does not say it is currently 66.

items.name: Support for Mortgage Interest
items.text: Must be a homeowner with a mortgage, loan or other charge on the property.
items.action: Replace 'other charge' with 'loan for certain home repairs or improvements'.
items.reason: Homeowners whose only secured borrowing is for something else, such as debt consolidation, could wrongly be told they qualify, while people with home improvement loans are not clearly told they are covered.

problems.claim: Must be a homeowner with a mortgage, loan or other charge on the property.
problems.note: A mortgage or home improvement loan is required, but the text never mentions an 'other charge' on the property.

items.name: State Pension claim
items.text: Must have reached State Pension age (currently 66 for men and women).
items.action: Remove 'currently 66' and point people to the State Pension age checker.
items.reason: State Pension age is rising above 66 for people born after 5 April 1960, so they could be told the wrong age at which they can claim.

problems.claim: Must have reached State Pension age (currently 66 for men and women).
problems.note: The text says you must reach State Pension age but never says that age is 66.

items.name: State Pension claim
items.text: Need at least 10 qualifying years of NI contributions or credits to receive any State Pension; 35 years for the full amount.
items.action: Limit the 35-year full-amount rule to records that started after April 2016 and add the contracted-out exception.
items.reason: The 10-year minimum is correct, but people who were contracted out or have pre-2016 records may wrongly expect the full amount after 35 years.

problems.claim: Need at least 10 qualifying years of NI contributions or credits to receive any State Pension; 35 years for the full amount.
problems.note: The 10-year minimum, counting contributions or credits, is stated. But 35 years for the full amount applies only to records that started after April 2016; contracted-out people usually need more than 35.

items.name: Voluntary National Insurance contributions (Class 3)
items.text: You have gaps in your National Insurance record that would increase your State Pension if filled.
items.action: Reword so having gaps is the condition, and tell people to check whether paying will increase their pension.
items.reason: Anyone with gaps can pay, so people whose pension would not go up could be wrongly told they don't qualify, including those paying to protect other benefits.

problems.claim: You have gaps in your National Insurance record that would increase your State Pension if filled.
problems.note: The text requires gaps and tells you to check whether paying will help, but it does not make an increase to your pension a condition of paying.

items.name: Winter Fuel Payment
items.text: Must usually live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, and be there in the qualifying week of 21 to 27 September 2026.
items.action: Remove the requirement to be physically present in England, Wales or Northern Ireland during the qualifying week.
items.reason: People who usually live there but were away during the qualifying week, for example on holiday, could be wrongly told they don't qualify.

problems.claim: Must usually live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, and be there in the qualifying week of 21 to 27 September 2026.
problems.note: Usual residence and the qualifying week dates are stated, but the text never says you must be physically present in England, Wales or Northern Ireland during the qualifying week.

items.name: Free bus pass
items.text: Must have reached State Pension age (currently 66). Some disabled people may also qualify before this age.
items.action: Cite the State Pension age page for the figure 66, or link to the State Pension age checker, noting that it is rising to 67.
items.reason: 66 is correct at the moment, but State Pension age depends on date of birth and is rising, so people nearing it could get the wrong date they qualify.

problems.claim: Must have reached State Pension age (currently 66). Some disabled people may also qualify before this age.
problems.note: The text supports State Pension age, and it supports some people getting the pass sooner ('check if you can get one sooner', plus the disabled pass), but it never gives the figure 66.

items.name: Rate Rebate
items.text: Must be liable for domestic rates in Northern Ireland.
items.action: Add that tenants can qualify when either they or their landlord is liable for rates.
items.reason: Tenants whose landlord pays the rates would wrongly be told they do not qualify.

problems.claim: Must be liable for domestic rates in Northern Ireland.
problems.note: The text requires homeowners to be liable, but for tenants either the tenant or the landlord can be liable, so the applicant does not always have to be liable themselves.

items.name: Funeral Support Payment
items.text: The funeral must take place in the UK, and applicant must live in Scotland.
items.action: Cite the official funeral location rule and add any exceptions, such as funerals in the EEA or Switzerland.
items.reason: Most funerals are in the UK, but people holding a funeral abroad under an exception could be wrongly told they do not qualify.

problems.claim: The funeral must take place in the UK, and applicant must live in Scotland.
problems.note: Living in Scotland is stated, but the text never says the funeral must be in the UK; it only limits transport help to travel within the UK.

items.name: Bereavement Support Payment
items.text: Must have been under State Pension age (66) at the time of the partner's death.
items.action: Cite the official State Pension age page for the age of 66 and say it is rising to 67.
items.reason: 66 is right for most deaths today, but State Pension age is rising, so a fixed figure could wrongly include or exclude people near the threshold whose partner dies later.

problems.claim: Must have been under State Pension age (66) at the time of the partner's death.
problems.note: The source says under State Pension age but does not give the age as 66.

items.name: Bereavement Support Payment
items.text: Deceased must have paid at least 25 weeks of Class 1 or 2 NI contributions, or died from a work-related accident or disease.
items.action: Cite the official guidance for the 25-week figure and add that the contributions must be in a single tax year.
items.reason: Without 'in one tax year', people whose partner paid 25 weeks spread over several years with no single qualifying year could be wrongly told they qualify.

problems.claim: Deceased must have paid at least 25 weeks of Class 1 or 2 NI contributions, or died from a work-related accident or disease.
problems.note: The source says 'a certain amount' of contributions and does not give a figure of 25 weeks; the work accident or disease alternative is stated.

items.name: Funeral Expenses Payment
items.text: You or your partner must be receiving Universal Credit, Pension Credit, Income Support, income-based JSA, income-related ESA, Housing Benefit, or the child tax credit and working tax credit element at the maximum rate.
items.action: Replace the list with the qualifying benefits exactly as the official page gives them, and remove the garbled tax credit wording.
items.reason: People on Income Support, income-based JSA or tax credits could be wrongly told they qualify. The tax credit condition as written is not a real rule.

problems.claim: You or your partner must be receiving Universal Credit, Pension Credit, Income Support, income-based JSA, income-related ESA, Housing Benefit, or the child tax credit and working tax credit element at the maximum rate.
problems.note: UC, income-related ESA, Pension Credit and Housing Benefit are listed, but Income Support, income-based JSA and tax credits are not in the text.

items.name: Funeral Expenses Payment
items.text: You are responsible for the funeral costs of a partner, close relative, or close friend where there is no other close relative able to pay.
items.action: Reword the rule to match the official conditions about the deceased's partner and close relatives who work or aren't on a qualifying benefit.
items.reason: Claimants whose case depends on the partner rule, or on another relative's work or benefit status, could be judged eligible or ineligible wrongly because 'able to pay' isn't the real test.

problems.claim: You are responsible for the funeral costs of a partner, close relative, or close friend where there is no other close relative able to pay.
problems.note: The text covers partners and close relatives or friends, but its conditions are about the deceased having no partner or the partner being unable to claim, and a close relative who is working or not on a qualifying benefit may stop you getting the payment. It does not say 'no other close relative able to pay'.

items.name: Tell Us Once
items.text: Death registered in England, Scotland or most of Wales (not available in all areas).
items.action: Say the service covers people who lived in England, Scotland or Wales, and remove 'most of Wales' and the claim that some areas are excluded.
items.reason: Families of people who lived in Wales could wrongly be told they may not qualify, and tying eligibility to where the death was registered rather than where the person lived could mislead some users.

problems.claim: Death registered in England, Scotland or most of Wales (not available in all areas).
problems.note: The text ties eligibility to where the person lived (England, Scotland or Wales) and to the death being registered or reported to a coroner; it does not say 'most of Wales' or that some areas are excluded.

items.name: Register the death
items.text: A person has died in England or Wales.
items.action: Cite the page that limits this route to England and Wales, and add the routes for deaths abroad, in Scotland and in Northern Ireland.
items.reason: Most people registering a death in England or Wales are unaffected, but anyone dealing with a death abroad or in Scotland or Northern Ireland could be wrongly told the service doesn't apply to them or not sent to the right route.

problems.claim: A person has died in England or Wales.
problems.note: The page covers deaths in the UK or abroad but never limits the service to deaths in England or Wales, so that restriction is not in the text.

items.name: Apply for probate
items.text: Person has died leaving assets held in their sole name.
items.action: Cite an official page that links probate to assets in the person's sole name, or reword the condition to match the source.
items.reason: Making 'sole name' a strict condition could wrongly screen out people who need probate for jointly held assets, such as property owned as tenants in common.

problems.claim: Person has died leaving assets held in their sole name.
problems.note: The text refers to a person who has died and suggests jointly owned assets may not need probate, but it never mentions 'sole name' or makes this a stated condition.

items.name: National Insurance number
items.text: UK citizens are automatically assigned one — applies mainly to non-UK nationals who have arrived to work or study.
items.action: Limit automatic issue to UK residents with a Child Benefit claim and remove the 'mainly non-UK nationals' claim.
items.reason: UK citizens with no Child Benefit claim made for them could be wrongly told they already have a number and don't need to apply.

problems.claim: UK citizens are automatically assigned one — applies mainly to non-UK nationals who have arrived to work or study.
problems.note: Automatic issue is only described for UK residents where a Child Benefit claim was made, not for all UK citizens, and the text never says the service is mainly for non-UK nationals arriving to work or study.

items.name: British citizenship (naturalisation)
items.text: Must be of good character (no serious criminal record) and demonstrate knowledge of English, Welsh or Scottish Gaelic.
items.action: Remove the 'no serious criminal record' definition, or replace it with the official good character guidance, which also covers immigration breaches, tax affairs and deception.
items.reason: People with minor convictions, immigration breaches or unpaid tax could be wrongly told they meet the good character requirement, and people with some old convictions could be wrongly put off.

problems.claim: Must be of good character (no serious criminal record) and demonstrate knowledge of English, Welsh or Scottish Gaelic.
problems.note: The source states good character and the language requirement, but it does not define good character as having no serious criminal record.

items.name: Citizenship ceremony
items.text: Adults aged 18 and over must attend in person. Children under 18 can be included on a parent's ceremony.
items.action: Cite the ceremony guidance for in-person attendance and for how children under 18 are treated, or remove the claim about children.
items.reason: Parents could be misled about whether their children under 18 must attend or are covered by the parent's ceremony. Adults are correctly told they must attend.

problems.claim: Adults aged 18 and over must attend in person. Children under 18 can be included on a parent's ceremony.
problems.note: The text says people aged 18 or over must attend, but it never says 'in person' and says nothing about adding children under 18 to a parent's ceremony.

items.name: View or prove your immigration status
items.text: Must have a UKVI account with an eVisa or EU Settlement Scheme status.
items.action: Cite the official guidance saying EU Settlement Scheme status can be viewed and proved through a UKVI account.
items.reason: EU Settlement Scheme status holders are told they qualify under a separate route, and only that group would be misled if the route were wrong.

problems.claim: Must have a UKVI account with an eVisa or EU Settlement Scheme status.
problems.note: The text says you need a UKVI account and an eVisa, but it never mentions EU Settlement Scheme status as another qualifying route.

items.name: Visa / leave to enter
items.text: Non-UK, non-Irish national wishing to enter the UK (some nationalities require visa; others may enter visa-free for short stays).
items.action: Cite the check-if-you-need-a-visa guidance for visa-free short stays and mention the ETA requirement.
items.reason: Visa-free short stays are real, but leaving out the ETA could mislead visa-free visitors who still need permission to travel.

problems.claim: Non-UK, non-Irish national wishing to enter the UK (some nationalities require visa; others may enter visa-free for short stays).
problems.note: The text covers people who are not British or Irish and says they may need a visa or an ETA, but it never says outright that some nationalities can enter visa-free for short stays.

items.name: Electoral roll update
items.text: Must be 16 or over to register (18 to vote in most elections).
