problems.claim: It was introduced from 2023.
problems.note: None of the sources gives a date of introduction.

items.name: File annual accounts at Companies House
items.text: All limited companies incorporated in the UK must file annual accounts at Companies House within 9 months of their financial year end. Small companies may file abridged or micro-entity accounts. From 1 April 2028 accounts must be filed using commercial software.
items.action: Limit the 9-month deadline to private companies, say abridged accounts need all members to agree, and tie micro-entity accounts to the micro-entity thresholds.
items.reason: Public companies could get the wrong deadline, and small companies above the micro-entity thresholds, or without every member's agreement, could file a type of accounts they are not allowed to use.

problems.claim: All limited companies incorporated in the UK must file annual accounts at Companies House within 9 months of their financial year end.
problems.note: The 9-month deadline is given for private limited companies; the text does not say it covers all UK-incorporated limited companies.
problems.quote: File annual accounts with Companies House 9 months after your company’s financial year ends

problems.claim: Small companies may file abridged or micro-entity accounts.
problems.note: The text supports abridged accounts for small companies, but only if all members agree, and it says micro-entity accounts are for companies that meet the separate micro-entity thresholds, not small companies in general.
problems.quote: If your company is small, you can: use the exemption so your company’s accounts do not need to be audited choose whether or not to send a copy of the director’s report and profit and loss account to Companies House send abridged accounts to Companies House

items.name: Register limited company (IN01)
items.text: Anyone can register a limited company in the UK. Registering online costs £100 and usually takes up to 24 hours. Company name must be available and not too similar to existing names. At least one director required.
items.action: Replace 'anyone can register' with the director limits: minimum age 16, and court permission needed for disqualified people.
items.reason: Under-16s and disqualified people would wrongly be told they can register, though most adult applicants are not affected.

problems.claim: Anyone can register a limited company in the UK.
problems.note: The text never says anyone can register, and it sets limits on directors, such as a minimum age of 16 and court permission for disqualified people.

items.name: Construction Industry Scheme (CIS) registration
items.text: Required for any business that pays subcontractors for construction work. Contractors must register before their first subcontractor payment. Subcontractors should register to have 20% deductions rather than 30%.
items.action: Change 'any business' to say registration is required unless an exception applies, and list the exceptions from the official page, such as work paid for by a charity.
items.reason: Most contractors and subcontractors get the right answer, but people whose work falls under an exception, such as work paid for by a charity, would be wrongly told they must register.

problems.claim: CIS registration is required for any business that pays subcontractors for construction work.
problems.note: The text requires registration for those who pay subcontractors, but it also lists exceptions where CIS does not apply (for example, work paid for by a charity), so 'any business' goes too far.
problems.quote: You must register as a contractor with the Construction Industry Scheme ( CIS ) if: you pay subcontractors to do construction work

items.name: Get an EORI number
items.text: Required for all UK businesses that import or export goods. Businesses with a UK VAT number can get an EORI number almost instantly online. Non-VAT-registered businesses can also apply.
items.action: Replace 'required for all' with 'may need' and list the exceptions, and remove the claim that a VAT number means an instant result.
items.reason: Most businesses moving goods to or from Great Britain do need an EORI, but those covered by the exceptions could be told they need one when they don't, and applicants could expect an instant number when HMRC checks can take up to 5 working days.

problems.claim: An EORI number is required for all UK businesses that import or export goods.
problems.note: The text requires a GB EORI for moving goods to or from Great Britain, but it mostly says you 'may need' one and lists exceptions, so it never says every UK importing or exporting business needs one.
problems.quote: If you move goods to or from Great Britain you must get an EORI number that starts with GB.

problems.claim: Businesses with a UK VAT number can get an EORI number almost instantly online.
problems.note: The text says a GB EORI is issued immediately unless HMRC needs to make checks, which can take up to 5 working days, but it does not link the quick result to having a VAT number.
problems.quote: You’ll get your GB EORI number immediately unless HMRC needs to make any checks on your application. If they do, it can take up to 5 working days.

items.name: Machine Games Duty registration
items.text: Mandatory for anyone operating dutiable gaming machines (fruit machines, AWPs, Category B/C/D) on premises with a gambling licence, alcohol licence, gaming machine permit or club certificate. Register at least 14 days before machines go live. File quarterly returns and pay within 30 days.
items.action: Cite the HMRC Machine Games Duty notice for the AWP and Category B/C/D terms, or reword to say 'dutiable machines' and note the exclusions.
items.reason: Listing Category D machines as dutiable could make some operators think they must register low-prize machines that are actually outside the duty (for example, where the top prize is no more than the cost to play), though most fruit machine operators would not be affected.

problems.claim: Machine Games Duty is mandatory for anyone operating dutiable gaming machines such as fruit machines, AWPs and Category B/C/D machines.
problems.note: The text mentions slot, fruit and quiz machines but never mentions AWPs or Category B/C/D machines.
problems.quote: You may have to pay Machine Games Duty ( MGD ) if you have machines that give cash prizes (such as slot, fruit or quiz machines) on your premises.

items.name: Food hygiene registration
items.text: Any business that sells, cooks, stores, handles, prepares or distributes food must register with their local authority at least 28 days before opening. Free to register. Required for home bakers, market stalls, restaurants, and caterers.
items.action: Limit the 28-day rule to the nations the source covers, add Scotland's own route, and cite an official page saying registration is free.
items.reason: Food businesses in Scotland could be given a rule and route the source doesn't back up. The 'free' claim is probably accurate but has no source, and the named business types are only examples.

problems.claim: Registration must be done at least 28 days before opening.
problems.note: The 28-day rule is stated only for England, Wales and Northern Ireland, while the claim applies it to any business with no limit on where it is.
problems.quote: England, Wales and Northern Ireland You are required to register at least 28 days before trading.

problems.claim: It is free to register.
problems.note: The source never mentions a cost or says registration is free.

problems.claim: Registration is required for home bakers, market stalls, restaurants, and caterers.
problems.note: The source covers home-based businesses, stalls and customer-facing premises, but it never names caterers, and it does not name home bakers or restaurants directly.
problems.quote: It includes businesses trading from home, a mobile unit, or temporary premises such as a stall or van

items.name: Short-term let licence (Scotland)
items.text: Scotland has a mandatory short-term let licensing scheme run by local councils; a licence gives legal permission to let accommodation to guests. Planning permission may also be needed in control areas. England's registration scheme has been announced but is not yet operating, so there is currently nothing to register in England.
items.action: Cite Scottish planning guidance for control areas and a source for England's scheme status, or remove the England claims.
items.reason: Hosts in control areas need to know planning permission may be needed as well as a licence, and people letting in England could be misled if the claim that there is nothing to register is wrong.

problems.claim: Planning permission may also be needed in control areas.
problems.note: This only appears as a heading in the contents list, and the text never says planning permission may be needed in control areas.
problems.quote: Planning permission and control areas for short-term lets

problems.claim: England's registration scheme has been announced but is not yet operating.
problems.note: None of the sources mention England.

problems.claim: There is currently nothing to register in England.
problems.note: None of the sources mention registering in England.

items.name: Skip permit (public road)
items.text: Required whenever a skip is placed on a public road in England and Wales. The skip hire company typically obtains the permit, but individuals should confirm with their local council. Safety requirements: reflective markings, traffic cones, lamps at night, and contact details displayed. Fine up to £1,000 for missing safety markings.
items.action: Say that safety markings, cones and lamps may be required depending on council conditions, and drop the claim that you must confirm with the council who gets the permit.
items.reason: Calling the safety items fixed requirements could mislead people whose council sets different conditions, though most permits are handled by the skip company and the advice to check with the council changes nothing.

problems.claim: Individuals should confirm with their local council.
problems.note: The text tells you to contact the council for a licence and for the rules on lights, but it never says to confirm with the council who is responsible for getting the permit.
problems.quote: In some areas you’ll need to do it yourself.

problems.claim: Safety requirements include reflective markings, traffic cones, lamps at night and displayed contact details.
problems.note: The items are listed, but the text says you 'may need' them and they 'could' apply, so it does not call them fixed requirements.
problems.quote: You may need to put safety lights and markings on or around the skip. This could include: reflective markings traffic cones night-time safety lamps the name and telephone number of the skip hire company

items.name: Street trading licence
items.text: Required for most street trading in England and Wales. Holders of a valid pedlar's certificate may be exempt for itinerant trading. Councils can restrict or refuse applications and waiting lists may apply. Fine up to £1,000 for trading without a licence.
items.action: Change 'most street trading' to 'you may need a licence' and cite a source for the pedlar exemption being limited to valid certificates and itinerant trading.
items.reason: Traders may wrongly think a licence is almost always needed, and pedlars may get limits on their exemption that the checked page does not state.

problems.claim: A licence is required for most street trading in England and Wales.
problems.note: The text says you 'may need' a licence and does not say most street trading needs one.
problems.quote: You may need to get a licence to trade in the street in England and Wales

problems.claim: Holders of a valid pedlar's certificate may be exempt for itinerant trading.
problems.note: The text supports the possible pedlar's certificate exemption but does not limit it to itinerant trading or say the certificate must be valid.
problems.quote: You might not need a street trading licence if you have a pedlar’s certificate

items.name: Register as a childminder with Ofsted
items.text: Required for anyone aged 18 or over who wants to care for children under 8 in a domestic setting for more than 2 hours per day in exchange for payment. Registration takes up to 12 weeks and involves a suitability inspection by Ofsted.
items.action: Remove the domestic-setting limit and call it a registration visit that usually does not happen if you only look after children over 5.
items.reason: People who childmind outside their own home may wrongly think they do not need to register, and people who only look after over-5s may expect an inspection that usually will not happen.

problems.claim: The requirement is for care in a domestic setting.
problems.note: The text covers home-based childminding, but it also says registration is required for childminding outside the home, so the requirement is not limited to domestic settings.
problems.quote: You must register with Ofsted or a childminder agency to look after children in a place outside the home.

problems.claim: Registration involves a suitability inspection by Ofsted.
problems.note: The text describes a registration visit by an inspector, not a 'suitability inspection', and says you usually will not get one if you only look after children over 5.
problems.quote: An inspector will visit you to check: your identity and qualifications - including first aid qualifications your house and garden are safe for children

items.name: DBS check
items.text: A criminal record check required for roles involving work with children or vulnerable adults. Employers apply on behalf of the employee. Four levels: basic (anyone aged 16 or over), standard, enhanced, and enhanced with barred lists.
items.action: Remove 'required' and the limit to children or vulnerable adults, and say employers can check for any role.
items.reason: Saying a check is 'required' and limited to certain roles could mislead people and employers about whether they must or can get one, though the basic level for anyone aged 16 or over is still mentioned.

problems.claim: A criminal record check required for roles involving work with children or vulnerable adults.
problems.note: The text says more detailed checks are available for roles such as healthcare or childcare, but it never says a check is required, and it says employers can check for any role.
problems.quote: You can request a more detailed check for certain roles, for example in healthcare or childcare.

items.name: Employers' Liability Insurance
items.text: A legal requirement for virtually all businesses that employ staff. Must have at least £5 million cover. Certificate must be displayed at each workplace. Penalties of up to £2,500/day for non-compliance.
items.action: Change the display rule to say the certificate must be somewhere employees can access it, which can include a website or intranet.
items.reason: Employers with several sites or remote staff might think they need a physical certificate at every workplace, when showing it electronically is allowed.

problems.claim: The certificate must be displayed at each workplace.
problems.note: The text requires the certificate to be displayed where employees can access it, and a website or intranet counts, so there is no rule that it must be at each workplace.
problems.quote: display your EL certificate where employees can access it (for example at your workplace, on your website or work intranet)

items.name: Find government grants for business
items.text: Free-to-search database covering grants, loans and equity finance from central and local government. Eligibility varies by scheme — most target small businesses, start-ups or specific sectors.
items.action: Say that many schemes are limited to particular regions, drop the claim that all providers are central or local government, and remove 'free' and 'most' unless a source supports them.
items.reason: The summary leaves out regional restrictions and makes it sound like every scheme comes from government, so someone could assume a scheme is open to them or government-run when it is limited to another region or run by a non-government body like Big Issue Invest.

problems.claim: The database is free to search.
problems.note: The page never says searching is free; its only use of 'free' is about local support on Business.gov.uk and about individual schemes.

problems.claim: The schemes come from central and local government.
problems.note: The page does not say who provides the schemes, and some listed schemes (for example Big Issue Invest) are not described as government schemes.

problems.claim: Most schemes target small businesses, start-ups or specific sectors.
problems.note: Many listed schemes target SMEs, start-ups, sectors or regions, but the page never says 'most' do, and many are aimed at particular regions instead.
problems.quote: Loan fund for SMEs in the manufacturing supply chain who are looking for investment to grow and support job creation.

items.name: Check and challenge business rates
items.text: Available to business ratepayers in England who believe their property's rateable value on the rating list is incorrect. The Check, Challenge, Appeal process requires a business rates account.
items.action: Add Wales and remove the unsourced limit to ratepayers who believe their value is wrong.
items.reason: Ratepayers with property in Wales would wrongly be told the service is not for them, and people who only want to check their value might think they are excluded.

problems.claim: The service is available to business ratepayers in England who believe their property's rateable value on the rating list is incorrect.
problems.note: The text covers properties in England, and in Wales too, but it does not say the service is limited to ratepayers who think their value is wrong, and it does not mention a rating list.
problems.quote: Use this service to find the ‘rateable value’ of a property in England or Wales.

problems.claim: The Check, Challenge, Appeal process requires a business rates account.
problems.note: The text says to use a business rates valuation account to challenge, but it never names a Check, Challenge, Appeal process.
problems.quote: If you want to report a change to your property or challenge its rateable value, use your business rates valuation account .

items.name: Check long-term flood risk
items.text: Free service available to anyone checking a property address in England. Results show flood risk from rivers and the sea, surface water, groundwater and reservoirs.
items.action: Say the service checks an area rather than a property address, add that groundwater risk is shown only where data is available, and cite a source for 'free' or remove it.
items.reason: People checking a home may think they get a result for their own property, or expect groundwater risk where there is no data. The 'free' claim is probably true but has no source here.

problems.claim: The service is free.
problems.note: The service page does not mention cost; the 'free' statements on linked pages are about flood warnings and evidence letters, not this service.

problems.claim: It is available to anyone checking a property address in England.
problems.note: The source says you check an area in England but says nothing about property addresses or who can use the service.
problems.quote: the long term flood risk for an area in England

problems.claim: Results show flood risk from rivers and the sea, surface water, groundwater and reservoirs.
problems.note: All four sources of flooding are listed, but the source says groundwater is covered only where data is available, and the claim leaves that condition out.
problems.quote: rivers and the sea surface water reservoirs groundwater (where data is available)

items.name: Sign up for flood warnings
items.text: Free for anyone with a property in or near a flood-risk area in England. Warnings are issued by the Environment Agency and cover river, coastal and groundwater flooding. You can register multiple properties and contact methods.
items.action: Cite a source for registering more than one property and contact method, and remove 'near' unless a page supports it.
items.reason: Someone whose property is only near a flood-risk area could be told they qualify when they may not get warnings, though most users with an at-risk property are unaffected.

problems.claim: The service is free for anyone with a property in or near a flood-risk area in England.
problems.note: The text says the service is free for homes or organisations at risk, but does not mention properties 'near' a flood-risk area.
problems.quote: if your home or organisation in England is at risk of flooding. The service is free.

problems.note: The text never says you can register more than one property.

problems.claim: You can register multiple contact methods.
problems.note: The text says you can choose a call, text or email, but not that you can register more than one contact method.
problems.quote: you can choose to get a call, text or email

items.name: Lifetime ISA withdrawal
items.text: First-time buyers can use their LISA savings (including the 25% government bonus) to purchase a property. Conveyancer requests the funds directly from the ISA provider before completion.
items.action: Cite the official Lifetime ISA home-buying page for the conveyancer asking for the funds and the timing before completion.
items.reason: Buyers rely on this to know they don't have to ask the provider themselves. A wrong role or timing could delay the money reaching completion.

problems.claim: The conveyancer requests the funds directly from the ISA provider before completion.
problems.note: The text says the funds go directly to the conveyancer, but it does not say the conveyancer requests them or mention timing before completion.
problems.quote: you use a conveyancer or solicitor to act for you in the purchase - the ISA provider will pay the funds directly to them

items.name: Stamp Duty Land Tax return
items.text: A return must be filed within 14 days of completing a property purchase in England or Northern Ireland. The solicitor usually handles this. Must be filed even if no tax is due.
items.action: Say a return is needed for most purchases over £40,000 or when claiming relief, and list the exemptions.
items.reason: People with exempt transactions would wrongly think they must file, though the 14-day deadline and the solicitor's role are right for typical buyers.

problems.claim: The return must be filed even if no tax is due.
problems.note: The text requires a return with no tax due only for most such transactions or when claiming relief, and lists exemptions where no return is needed.
problems.quote: You must still send an SDLT return for most transactions under £150,000.

items.name: Search for property information
items.text: Anyone can search the Land Registry for information on registered properties in England and Wales. A title register or title plan costs £7. Useful when buying a property or checking ownership.
items.action: Remove the unsourced 'useful when buying' line and state that downloaded copies are not proof of ownership.
items.reason: People who need proof of ownership, for example for legal or official purposes, could pay £7 for a download that the page says is not proof, even though most users only need to look up details.

problems.claim: The search is useful when buying a property.
problems.note: The page never says the search is useful when buying a property.

problems.claim: The search is useful for checking ownership.
problems.note: The title register shows who owns the property, but the page says the downloaded copies are not proof of ownership, and it never calls the search useful for checking ownership.
problems.quote: You can download online copies of the information but you cannot use them as proof of ownership.

items.name: Land Registry registration (AP1)
items.text: All property purchases in England and Wales must be registered at HM Land Registry. Usually handled by the solicitor/conveyancer. Priority period starts when the application is received — must be submitted promptly after completion.
items.action: Add the short-lease exemption, say a solicitor 'may' apply, and remove the unsourced priority-period and timing claims.
items.reason: People with leases of 7 years or less are told wrongly that they must register, and self-applicants are given an unsourced account of how priority works that may be wrong.

problems.claim: All property purchases in England and Wales must be registered at HM Land Registry.
problems.note: The text says bought land or property must be registered, but short leases of 7 years or less are usually exempt, so 'all' goes too far.
problems.quote: You do not usually need to register leasehold land or property if there are 7 years or less on the lease when you take ownership.

problems.claim: The application is usually handled by the solicitor or conveyancer.
problems.note: The text says the solicitor 'may' apply; it does not say this usually happens.
problems.quote: If you’re a new owner, your solicitor or conveyancer may apply as part of the purchase.

problems.claim: The priority period starts when the application is received.
problems.note: None of the sources mention a priority period.

problems.claim: The application must be submitted promptly after completion.
problems.note: No deadline or timing for the registration application is given.

items.name: Check or challenge your council tax band
items.text: Anyone can check any property's council tax band for free. Property owners and tenants can challenge their band if they have evidence it is incorrectly assessed, for example if similar nearby properties are in a lower band.
items.action: Cite the official pages that say band checks are free and cover any property, name who can challenge and what evidence counts, and add that Scotland uses a separate website.
items.reason: Most people in England or Wales would still check and challenge correctly, but Scottish users are not told to use a different site, and the unsourced wording about who can challenge and what evidence counts could mislead some people about whether their case is worth making.

problems.claim: Anyone can check any property's council tax band.
problems.note: The text covers looking up a home's band in England or Wales, with Scotland handled on a separate website, but it never says anyone can check any property.
problems.quote: Find out the Council Tax band for a home in England or Wales by looking up its address or postcode. For homes in Scotland, search on the Scottish Assessors website.

problems.note: The text says nothing about cost.

items.name: Find a Job
items.text: Free to use for anyone looking for work in England, Scotland or Wales (Northern Ireland has a separate service). Employers post vacancies directly. Jobseekers can save searches and upload CVs.
items.action: Cite sources for free use and saved searches, and check the CV upload claim against the current service or remove it.
items.reason: Being free is almost certainly correct, but if CV upload is not a current feature, jobseekers could plan their applications around a tool that does not exist.

problems.claim: The service is free to use.
problems.note: None of the sources mention cost.

problems.note: None of the sources mention saving searches.

problems.claim: Jobseekers can upload CVs.
problems.note: None of the sources mention uploading CVs to Find a job.

items.name: PAYE Starter Checklist
items.text: Required when starting a new job without a P45 — whether first job, return after a gap, or an additional concurrent job. The employer provides the form; the employee self-declares their tax situation, student loan plan type, and whether they are receiving any benefits. items.action: Say the checklist is on GOV.UK (online or printable) and the employer asks for it, and drop or cite the emergency tax code claim.
items.reason: New starters may wait for the employer to hand them a form instead of getting it from GOV.UK. The emergency tax claim is unsourced.

problems.claim: Without it, the employer must apply an emergency tax code.
problems.note: None of the sources mention an emergency tax code.

items.name: Apply for bankruptcy
items.text: Available to individuals in England and Wales who cannot pay their debts. Apply online only; the £680 fee can be paid in instalments but must be paid before submitting. Bankruptcy typically lasts one year, after which most remaining debts are written off.
items.action: Cite the official pages for the 'cannot pay your debts' condition, the one-year length and the writing-off of debts.
items.reason: Being unable to pay is a qualifying condition, and the length and outcome shape what applicants expect, so an error here could mislead some people even though these claims look accurate.

problems.claim: It is for people who cannot pay their debts.
problems.note: The text mentions debt but does not state inability to pay as a condition.
problems.quote: check other options for dealing with debt

problems.claim: Bankruptcy typically lasts one year.
problems.note: The text does not say how long bankruptcy lasts.

problems.claim: After bankruptcy, most remaining debts are written off.
problems.note: The text does not mention debts being written off.

items.name: Breathing Space (debt respite scheme)
items.text: Available to anyone in England or Wales with problem debt who seeks help from an FCA-authorised debt adviser. The adviser must apply on the client's behalf. During breathing space, creditors cannot chase debts, add interest or take enforcement action.
items.action: Replace 'anyone' with a reference to the eligibility conditions and cite a source for the FCA-authorised adviser requirement.
items.reason: Most people with problem debt in England or Wales will qualify, but people who fail a condition, such as having had a breathing space recently, could wrongly be told they qualify.

problems.note: The text supports England or Wales and getting debt advice, but for Breathing Space it never says the adviser must be FCA-authorised, and it lists eligibility conditions, so the scheme is not open to 'anyone'.
problems.quote: If you live in England or Wales, you can get temporary protection from your creditors while you get debt advice and make a plan.

items.name: Free Childcare (disadvantaged 2-year-olds)
items.text: 15 hours/week free childcare for eligible 2-year-olds in England. Qualifying criteria include receiving income-related benefits, being a looked-after child, having an EHC plan, receiving DLA, or leaving care.
items.action: Say that leaving care only counts when the child left under an adoption order, special guardianship order or child arrangements order.
items.reason: Families whose 2-year-old left care some other way, such as going back to their parents, could be told wrongly that they qualify. Most people applying through benefits are not affected.

problems.claim: Leaving care is one of the qualifying criteria.
problems.note: The source only counts leaving care under an adoption order, special guardianship order or child arrangements order, and the claim leaves out that condition.

items.name: Free NHS Dental Treatment
items.text: Free NHS dental treatment is available to: under-18s (or under-19 in full-time education), pregnant women and new mothers (12 months after birth), people on certain benefits, HC2 certificate holders, and War Pension dental scheme members.

items.text: Open to anyone. problems.quote: You may be able to get help paying for childcare that is registered with Ofsted.

items.name: Update HMRC records
items.text: Notify HMRC of any change to name, address or marital status. Affects tax code, correspondence and benefit entitlements. Required after moving, marriage, divorce or name change.

problems.claim: These changes affect correspondence.

items.name: Find an Ofsted inspection report
items.text: Free and open to anyone. Search by provider name, postcode, or Unique Reference Number (URN) to view the latest Ofsted report, rating, and any follow-up action required.
items.action: Replace "rating" with the report card wording the page uses, drop "follow-up action required", and cite a source for the free, open-access claim.
items.reason: Anyone can use a free search tool, so nobody would be wrongly turned away, but parents looking at a school would expect a single rating and follow-up actions that Ofsted's newer report cards may not show, so they could misread the result.

problems.claim: The service is free.
problems.note: The text says nothing about cost.

problems.claim: You can view the latest Ofsted report.

problems.note: The text does not mention ratings. It only mentions report cards in a link title.

problems.claim: You can view any follow-up action required.
problems.note: The text does not mention follow-up action.

items.name: Provisional Driving Licence
items.text: Required before you can take driving lessons or book a theory or practical test. Apply from age 15 years and 9 months so it arrives by your 17th birthday. Costs £34 online or £43 by post. Must be resident in Great Britain for at least 185 days in the last 12 months and be able to read a number plate from 20 metres.
items.action: Replace 'resident for 185 days in the last 12 months' with the official wording about 185 days' permission to live in Great Britain.
items.reason: Applicants who recently came back from abroad, or non-UK nationals, could be told wrongly that they don't qualify because of a 12-month residence test the page does not state.

problems.claim: The licence is required before you can take driving lessons or book a theory or practical test.
problems.note: The text does not say this.

problems.claim: Applying at that age means it arrives by your 17th birthday.
problems.note: The text never mentions the licence arriving by a 17th birthday.

problems.claim: You must have been resident in Great Britain for at least 185 days in the last 12 months.
problems.note: The text gives 185 days of permission to live in Great Britain, but it does not say 'in the last 12 months'.
problems.quote: have been given permission to live in Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales) for at least 185 days

items.name: Notify DVLA of vehicle sale
items.text: When selling or transferring a vehicle, the seller must notify DVLA online immediately. The green new keeper slip from the V5C goes to the buyer. Vehicle tax is not transferred — the buyer must tax the vehicle before driving it (or make a SORN). If no V5C exists, the buyer must apply for one using form V62 (£25).
items.action: Add the postal route for sellers without a log book, and cite a source for 'immediately' or soften it.
items.reason: Sellers without a V5C log book are only pointed to the online route and miss the postal route they need. The 'immediately' wording is probably accurate but isn't sourced.

problems.claim: When selling or transferring a vehicle, the seller must notify DVLA online immediately.
problems.note: The text says to tell DVLA and offers an online service, but it never says 'immediately' and it also describes a postal route for sellers without a log book.
problems.quote: Tell DVLA when you no longer own a vehicle

items.name: Tax your vehicle
items.text: Any vehicle driven or kept on a public road must be taxed. Requires a V5C in your name (or the green new keeper slip if recently purchased), a valid MOT for most vehicles, and valid insurance. Pay annually or by monthly Direct Debit. Amount depends on vehicle type, age, and CO2 emissions. Exempt vehicles must still be declared.
items.action: Add the tax reminder or warning letter reference as an alternative to the V5C, and say insurance evidence is only needed at a Post Office in Northern Ireland.
items.reason: Keepers who have a reminder letter but no V5C in hand may wrongly think they can't tax, and people outside Northern Ireland are told insurance is a requirement for taxing.

problems.claim: Any vehicle driven or kept on a public road must be taxed.
problems.note: The text covers driving, but it does not mention vehicles kept on a public road.
problems.quote: It’s illegal to drive your vehicle until you’ve taxed it.

problems.claim: You need a V5C in your name, or the green new keeper slip if you recently bought the vehicle.
problems.note: The text also accepts a reference number from a recent tax reminder or warning letter, so a V5C or green slip is not strictly required.
problems.quote: your vehicle log book (V5C) - it must be in your name the green ‘new keeper’ slip from a log book if you’ve just bought it

problems.claim: Most vehicles need a valid MOT.
problems.note: The text says you 'might' need a valid MOT, but it does not say this applies to 'most vehicles'.
problems.quote: You might also need to show evidence of an MOT (it must be valid when the tax starts).

problems.claim: You need valid insurance.
problems.note: Insurance evidence is only named as a requirement for taxing at a Post Office in Northern Ireland.
problems.quote: To tax your vehicle at a Post Office in Northern Ireland, you’ll also need both: a paper copy of an insurance certificate or cover note

problems.claim: The amount depends on vehicle type, age and CO2 emissions.
problems.note: The text does not say what the tax amount depends on.

items.name: Driving Test (practical)
items.text: Must pass the theory test before the practical test can be booked. Costs £62 (weekday) or £75 (evening/weekend/bank holiday). On passing, DVLA usually sends the full licence automatically — but if you did not hand your provisional to the examiner, or your name/address has changed, you must apply with form D1 within 2 years. Must be resident in Great Britain for at least 185 days in the last 12 months.
items.action: Cite the DVLA guidance on form D1 and on name or address changes, and describe automatic sending as an option the examiner offers.
items.reason: Form D1 and the name/address rule are probably correct but unsourced, and calling automatic sending usual could confuse people who did not hand over their provisional licence.

problems.claim: When you pass, DVLA usually sends the full licence automatically.
problems.note: The source presents automatic sending as an option, not the usual outcome, and does not name DVLA.
problems.quote: ask you if you want your full licence to be sent to you automatically - give the examiner your provisional licence if you want to do this

problems.claim: If your name or address has changed, you must apply for the licence yourself.
problems.note: The source does not mention a change of name or address.

problems.claim: You apply using form D1.
problems.note: The source does not name form D1.

items.name: Theory Test
items.text: All learner drivers must pass a theory test before they can book a practical driving test. Costs £23. Consists of 50 multiple-choice questions and a hazard perception video clip test. Pass certificate is valid for 2 years — if you do not pass the practical test within 2 years you must retake the theory. Must be resident in Great Britain for at least 185 days in the last 12 months.
items.action: Replace 'All learner drivers' with 'usually' and list the exceptions, such as automatic-to-manual upgrades and tractor and taxi tests.
items.reason: Most learner drivers do need the theory test, but some people, such as those upgrading from an automatic to a manual licence, would be wrongly told they must take it.

problems.claim: All learner drivers must pass a theory test before they can book a practical driving test.
problems.note: The source says 'usually' and lists exceptions (e.g. automatic-to-manual upgrades, tractor and taxi tests), so 'all' goes further than the text.
problems.quote: You must usually have passed your theory test before booking.

items.name: Check and pay Clean Air Zone charges
items.text: Applies to drivers of non-compliant vehicles (typically pre-Euro 6 diesel or pre-Euro 4 petrol) entering Clean Air Zones in cities such as Bath, Birmingham, Bradford and Portsmouth. Charges vary by zone and vehicle type.
items.action: Cite the official vehicle compliance guidance for the Euro 6 diesel and Euro 4 petrol thresholds and for how charges vary by zone and vehicle type.
items.reason: The Euro thresholds are hedged with "typically" and are broadly accurate, but they decide who has to pay, and some drivers could be misled (for example, private car drivers in zones that don't charge cars).

problems.claim: Non-compliant vehicles are typically pre-Euro 6 diesel or pre-Euro 4 petrol.
problems.note: The text does not mention Euro standards or fuel types.

problems.claim: Charges vary by zone and vehicle type.
problems.note: The text gives no charge amounts and does not say how charges vary.

items.name: Basic DBS criminal record check
items.text: Anyone aged 16 or over can apply for a basic DBS check on themselves. Costs £21.50. Shows only unspent convictions. For people working in England and Wales; people in Scotland or Northern Ireland can also apply. Distinct from standard and enhanced checks, which are only available for specific roles and applied for by employers.
items.action: Say that people in Scotland or Northern Ireland can apply only if the job is in England or Wales, and note that self-employed people and personal employees can apply for enhanced checks themselves.
items.reason: People in Scotland or Northern Ireland with a job there could be sent to apply for a DBS basic check instead of using their own nation's process, and self-employed people could wrongly think they can't apply for an enhanced check themselves.

problems.claim: People in Scotland or Northern Ireland can also apply.
problems.note: People there can apply only if the job is in England or Wales, a condition the claim leaves out; jobs in Scotland or Northern Ireland use a different process.
problems.quote: You can also get a basic DBS check if you live in Northern Ireland or Scotland but the job you’re applying for is in England or Wales.

problems.claim: Standard and enhanced checks are applied for by employers.
problems.note: Employers do run standard and enhanced checks, but Source 2 says self-employed people and personal employees can apply for an enhanced check themselves, so these checks are not applied for only by employers.
problems.quote: As an employer or Registered Body, you provide the candidate with a DBS application form to complete and return to you.

items.name: View and share driving licence
items.text: Available if your licence was issued in England, Wales or Scotland; Northern Ireland has a separate service. Lets you see your entitlements, any penalty points, and driving test passes. Generates a one-time check code valid for 21 days.
items.action: Remove 'one-time' and the unsourced mention of driving test passes, and cite a source for the separate Northern Ireland service.
items.reason: Calling the code one-time could make people think a code is used up after one check, or generate extra codes they don't need. The unsourced claim that test passes are shown could set wrong expectations.

problems.claim: Northern Ireland has a separate service.
problems.note: The page only links to 'Northern Ireland driving licences' and does not say there is a separate view-and-share service.
problems.quote: Elsewhere on the web Northern Ireland driving licences

problems.claim: The service lets you see driving test passes.
problems.note: The text never mentions driving test passes.

problems.claim: The service generates a one-time check code valid for 21 days.
problems.note: The 21-day validity is stated, but the text never says the code is one-time.
problems.quote: The check code will be valid for 21 days.

items.name: Vehicle Enquiry Service
items.text: Free service available to anyone with a UK vehicle registration number. Shows whether the vehicle has a current MOT, is taxed, the colour, fuel type and year of manufacture.
items.action: Cite an official source for the service being free and showing colour, and for the UK registration number requirement, or remove those claims.
items.reason: The unsourced 'free' claim is about cost and could mislead users if it were wrong, though it is very likely accurate. The colour and 'anyone' wording would not change what users do.

problems.claim: The service is free.

problems.claim: It shows the vehicle's colour.
problems.note: Colour is not in the list of details the online service shows. It appears only under 'Contact DVLA', which is described as another way to check.

items.name: Check MOT history
items.text: Free service for any vehicle that has had an MOT in Great Britain. Useful when buying a used car to check for recurrent failures or odometer discrepancies.
items.action: Say the history covers Northern Ireland as well as Great Britain, and only from 2005 for cars, motorcycles and vans or 2018 for HGVs, trailers, buses and coaches.
items.reason: People with vehicles tested in Northern Ireland could wrongly think they can't use the service, and people wanting tests from before 2005 or 2018 could expect records that don't exist. The unsourced 'free' claim and used-car advice don't change what anyone does.

problems.claim: The service is free.
problems.note: The text says nothing about cost.

problems.claim: The service covers any vehicle that has had an MOT in Great Britain.
problems.note: The text covers tests in Great Britain, but only from 2005 or 2018 depending on vehicle type, and it also covers Northern Ireland, so it is neither 'any' vehicle nor Great Britain only.
problems.quote: If you got your test in England, Scotland or Wales

problems.claim: It can be used to check for recurrent failures or odometer discrepancies.
problems.note: The text does not mention recurrent failures or odometer discrepancies.

items.name: Pay a court fine
items.text: Anyone who has received a fine from a magistrates court and has a payment reference number can pay online.
items.action: Limit the service to England and Wales, point Scotland and Northern Ireland to their own ways to pay, warn that payments may be rejected once enforcement has started, and replace 'payment reference' with the notice of fine and a card.
items.reason: People with fines in Scotland or Northern Ireland, and people whose fine has gone to enforcement, would wrongly be told they can pay through this service, though most people in England and Wales would not be affected.

problems.claim: Anyone who has received a fine from a magistrates court can pay online.
problems.note: The page limits the service to England and Wales, points to different ways to pay in Scotland and Northern Ireland, and warns that a payment may be rejected if enforcement has started, so 'anyone' is too broad.

problems.claim: Paying online requires a payment reference number.
problems.note: The page says you need the notice of fine and a card; it does not mention a payment reference number.
problems.quote: You need your ‘notice of fine’ and a debit or credit card.

items.name: Respond to a jury summons
items.text: People on the electoral register aged 18 to 75 who have lived in the UK for at least 5 years can be called for jury service in England and Wales. You must respond within 7 days of getting the summons, even if you are disqualified. You can ask to change the date or be excused. For the first 10 days you can claim up to £64.95 a day for loss of earnings or care costs (more than 4 hours at court) plus £5.71 for food and drink, and travel costs.
items.action: Add that the 5 years must be continuous, must come after age 13, and can include time in the Channel Islands or Isle of Man.
items.reason: Most people will be classed correctly, but some will be classed wrongly: those whose 5 years had gaps or started before age 13 could be told they qualify when they don't, and those who lived in the Channel Islands or Isle of Man could be told they don't qualify when they do.

problems.claim: You must have lived in the UK for at least 5 years to be called.
problems.note: The 5-year figure matches, but the source adds conditions the claim leaves out: the 5 years must have no gaps and must come after age 13, and the Channel Islands and Isle of Man also count.
problems.quote: have lived in the UK, Channel Islands or Isle of Man for at least 5 years without any gaps - this must be after the age of 13

items.name: Report a lost or stolen passport
items.text: Anyone whose UK passport has been lost or stolen should cancel it immediately. A replacement must then be applied for separately.
items.action: Cite the official page saying a replacement must be applied for separately, and word it as needed only if the person wants a replacement.
items.reason: The point that cancelling does not replace the passport is correct and useful, but 'must' could make someone who doesn't need a passport think they have to apply and pay for one.

problems.claim: A replacement must then be applied for separately.
problems.note: The text says you cancel before applying for a replacement, so the replacement is a separate later step, but it never says you must apply for one.
problems.quote: If your passport has been lost or stolen, you must cancel it before applying for a replacement.

items.name: Visit someone in prison
items.text: Family members and friends of prisoners can book visits. The prisoner must first add the visitor to their approved visitor list. ID may be required.
items.action: Cite the official page on what ID visitors must bring, and say ID is required instead of that it 'may be required'.
items.reason: Visitors are commonly turned away without acceptable ID, so the hedged 'may be required' could lead some to arrive without it. The 'family and friends' framing is mostly harmless for typical visitors, but it swaps the real condition (being on the visitor list) for a relationship test.

problems.claim: Family members and friends of prisoners can book visits.
problems.note: The text says you can book a visit for yourself or someone else, but it never says visitors are family members or friends; the condition it gives is being on the visitor list.
problems.quote: You can make a booking for yourself or for someone else.

problems.claim: ID may be required.
problems.note: None of the sources mention ID being needed for a visit.

items.name: Appeal a planning decision
items.text: Available to anyone who has had a planning application refused by their local council, or where the council failed to decide within the statutory timeframe. Time limits vary by appeal type (12 weeks for householder appeals, 6 months for most others).
items.action: Change the 12-week limit so it covers only householder refusals, and state 6 months for householder non-determination and conditions appeals.
items.reason: People appealing a householder non-determination or conditions decision would be given a 12-week deadline instead of 6 months, while the typical householder refusal case is correct.

problems.claim: The time limit is 12 weeks for householder appeals.
problems.note: The 12-week limit only covers householder refusals; the same table gives 6 months for householder non-determination and for conditions.
problems.quote: An appeal against refusal of a householder planning application (See 4.4 for what counts as a householder application) We must receive the appeal within 12 weeks from the date on the decision notice

items.name: ACAS early conciliation
items.text: Mandatory pre-tribunal step for most employment disputes; a free Acas conciliation service that tries to resolve disputes before a tribunal claim is lodged.
items.action: Reword to say notifying Acas is mandatory for most claims but taking part in conciliation is voluntary, and cite the Acas page confirming the service is free.
items.reason: Claimants, and employers especially, may think they have to take part in conciliation when only the notification is required, which could affect how they respond. The 'free' claim is probably accurate but needs a source.

problems.claim: Early conciliation is a mandatory pre-tribunal step for most employment disputes.
problems.note: Notifying Acas is mandatory and some claims are exempt, but the text says taking part in conciliation itself is voluntary, so only the notification is a required step.
problems.quote: You must notify Acas if you want to make a claim to an employment tribunal.

problems.claim: The Acas early conciliation service is free.
problems.note: The text never says early conciliation is free; the only thing it calls free is the penalty enforcement scheme.

items.name: Child Maintenance Service
items.text: If parents cannot agree privately. CMS calculates based on paying parent's income.

items.reason: Parents who could agree but would rather use the CMS might think they can't use it, though the income basis is accurate and appears on other official pages.

problems.claim: The Child Maintenance Service is used if parents cannot agree privately.
problems.note: The text gives private arrangement (if both parents agree) and the CMS as two options, but it never says the CMS is only for parents who cannot agree.
problems.quote: privately between parents , if both parents agree through the Child Maintenance Service

problems.claim: CMS calculates based on the paying parent's income.
problems.note: The text says the CMS works out an amount to pay but does not say this is based on the paying parent's income.
problems.quote: work out an amount to pay

items.name: Renew driving licence at 70
items.text: From age 70 all driving licences expire and must be renewed every 3 years. Free online. Medical self-declaration required. Failure to renew makes driving unlawful.
items.action: Cite the official pages saying licences expire at 70, that renewal includes a medical self-declaration, and that driving without a valid licence is unlawful.
items.reason: Anyone working out their renewal deadline and steps relies on the claims about expiry at 70 and the self-declaration; these read as accurate but currently have no source.

problems.claim: From age 70 all driving licences expire.
problems.note: The text implies that renewal is due at 70, but it never says that every licence expires at age 70.
problems.quote: DVLA will automatically send you this form 90 days before your 70th birthday or before your licence expires.

problems.claim: A medical self-declaration is required.
problems.note: The text lists eyesight and fitness to drive as conditions for using the service, but it does not describe a self-declaration step.
problems.quote: you meet the minimum eyesight requirement you are not prevented from driving for any reason

problems.claim: Failure to renew makes driving unlawful.
problems.note: The text does not say what happens if you drive without renewing.

items.name: Access to Work
items.text: Grants for workplace adaptations, travel costs and support workers. Apply if you are in paid work, or about to start or return to paid work in the next 12 weeks.
items.action: Add that travel costs are covered only if you cannot use public transport.
items.reason: People who can use public transport may wrongly expect help with travel costs.

problems.claim: Access to Work provides grants for travel costs.
problems.note: The text covers travel costs only if you cannot use public transport, and the claim leaves that condition out.

items.name: Attendance Allowance
items.text: For over-65s with care needs. Not means-tested. Two rates depending on day/night needs.

problems.claim: Attendance Allowance is for over-65s with care needs.
problems.note: The text links eligibility to State Pension age and care needs but never gives the age 65.

items.name: Carer's Allowance
items.text: If caring 35+ hours/week and person cared for receives PIP or Attendance Allowance.

problems.note: The text only lists the PIP daily living component, not PIP in general.

items.text: Formal review of a DWP benefit decision. Must be requested before you can appeal to a tribunal. Apply within 1 month of the decision letter.
